title: Who hires accessibility reviewers, and why now
description: The actual categories of organisation that fund this work, and the obligations behind each first hire — because the pitch that lands depends on which category you're talking to.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the sectors and obligations that most reliably fund accessibility roles
Explain why a first accessibility hire at a given organisation exists

contentSections.title: Five kinds of employer, five different reasons

contentSections.body: A government benefits portal, a mid-size hospital system, a three-person e-commerce brand and a Fortune 500 bank all post an accessibility-related role in the same month. None of them are lying about needing the work. None of them need it for the same reason.

Nearly every organisation that funds accessibility QA sits in one of five overlapping categories:

- **Public sector and publicly funded** — government agencies, public universities, anyone receiving federal or state funds. Covered by Section 508 (US federal) or its state equivalents, and increasingly by binding digital-accessibility rules with real compliance deadlines.
- **Regulated or high-litigation-risk private sector** — banking, insurance, healthcare, large retail and hospitality. Covered by public-accommodation law (ADA Title III in the US) and the target of the large majority of digital accessibility lawsuits.
- **Anyone selling into the EU** — the European Accessibility Act applies to a wide range of digital products and services sold to EU consumers, regardless of where the company is based.
- **Consultancies and agencies** — sell accessibility expertise as the product itself, to all of the above.
- **Everyone else, opportunistically** — companies that hire because a founder cares, a customer complained, or a competitor got sued. Real work, thinner mandate, more vulnerable to being cut.

contentSections.question: Guess first: of the five categories above, which one is most likely to disappear entirely if a founder or one enthusiastic manager leaves?
contentSections.answer: "Everyone else, opportunistically" — the category with no external obligation behind it. The other four are backed by a law, a deadline, or a client contract, none of which resign when a person does.
contentSections.hint: Ask which category's justification lives in one person's head rather than in a regulation or contract.

contentSections.scenario: A university's student portal has failed an internal audit twice in two years, and this time the general counsel's office — not IT — is the one requesting budget for a permanent accessibility QA hire.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely root cause of counsel driving this rather than IT?

options.label: IT lost interest in the portal
A specific legal exposure has become concrete enough that it's now counsel's problem, not just an engineering backlog item
Universities always route accessibility work through legal

feedback.it: IT interest isn't really the variable here — IT rarely owns the budget decision to create a new permanent role regardless of their interest level.
feedback.legal: Right. When a request for permanent headcount comes from counsel rather than engineering, it usually means a specific risk has crystallised — a complaint, an OCR investigation, a near-miss lawsuit — that's now measured in dollars and treated as urgent rather than as backlog.
feedback.always: Not always — plenty of universities run accessibility work entirely through IT or a dedicated digital accessibility office with no legal involvement at all. The pattern here is specific to *this* signal (counsel requesting the budget), not a universal rule about the sector.

contentSections.mechanism: A role's funding source tells you what the organisation is actually afraid of, and that shapes what your first ninety days should focus on. A legally-driven hire needs documented, defensible findings fast. An engineering-driven hire has more room to build process first.

contentSections.body: This matters for more than curiosity. The category an organisation falls into tells you what to lead with in a pitch or interview: a healthcare system wants to hear about risk and patient-portal specifics; a startup that hired because a founder cares wants to hear about product quality and user trust; a consultancy wants to see that you can produce a defensible finding fast, for a client you've never met, on your first day.
Know which of the five categories you're talking to before you open your mouth — the pitch that lands is different for each one.

contentSections.title: Why the market looks different now than it did five years ago

contentSections.body: Someone who trained as an accessibility reviewer a decade ago describes a field that was almost entirely evangelism — convincing a reluctant team that this mattered at all. That is no longer the main job in most of the sectors above.

contentSections.scenario: Digital accessibility lawsuits filed in US federal court under Title III of the ADA have risen sharply over the last decade.
contentSections.question: Roughly how many such lawsuits were filed in a recent full year, order of magnitude?
contentSections.explanation: The precise count moves year to year and by whoever is counting, but the order of magnitude — several thousand federal digital-accessibility suits in a year, plus many more threatened demand letters that never reach a filing — is what matters for a job seeker. It means legal exposure is no longer a hypothetical argument you have to make to a skeptical hiring manager; it's an ambient fact most mid-size and large companies' legal departments already know.

contentSections.body:
Three concrete shifts, not vague ones:

1. **Litigation volume**, described above, has made "we could get sued" a live budget-line argument rather than a scare tactic.
2. **The European Accessibility Act's obligations reached full enforcement in mid-2025**, and any company selling digital products or services into the EU — including plenty of US-based SaaS companies with EU customers — now has to answer for it, whether or not accessibility was previously anyone's job there.
3. **US public-sector deadlines are concrete and dated.** The 2024 rule updating Title II of the ADA for state and local government web and app content set phased compliance deadlines running into 2026 and 2027 depending on population size — which is why public-sector hiring in this space has a visible bump timed to those dates.

contentSections.question: A hiring manager tells you flatly: "Honestly, we're only doing this because legal told us to." Guess first — is that a bad sign for the role, or close to irrelevant?
contentSections.answer: Close to irrelevant, and often a good sign. It tells you the funding is real and unlikely to be cut on a whim next quarter — which matters more day to day than *why* the budget line exists in the first place.
contentSections.hint: Ask what happens to a role's budget stability when its justification is a compliance deadline with a date attached, versus a manager's personal enthusiasm.

contentSections.body: The pitch that used to require convincing someone accessibility mattered now more often just requires naming the specific deadline or exposure that applies to them.

title: In-house, agency and freelance compared
description: What actually differs between the three main employment shapes this work comes in — pace, benefits, autonomy and what each one asks of your energy specifically.

learningObjectives.text: Compare in-house, agency and freelance routes on the dimensions that matter for a specific person's constraints

contentSections.title: Same skill, three very different jobs

contentSections.body: Two people with identical audit skill take different routes: one joins an insurance company's product team, one joins a twelve-person accessibility consultancy. A year later they'd struggle to swap roles without real onboarding — not because either lost the skill, but because the jobs pull on it completely differently.

contentSections.scenario:
In-house: you audit the same product for years, sit in sprint planning, and are measured partly on whether findings actually get fixed.

Agency: you audit a new, unfamiliar product every one to three weeks, for a client you may never meet twice, and are measured on billable hours and client satisfaction.

Freelance: you do a mix of both, but every client relationship, every contract and every collections conversation is yours alone to run.
contentSections.question: Which route gives you the most influence over whether your findings actually get fixed?

options.label: In-house
Agency
Freelance

feedback.inhouse: Right. Sitting in sprint planning and being measured on remediation, not just findings, means you're present for the fights about prioritisation — and that's real influence an outside reviewer structurally can't have.
feedback.agency: An agency reviewer hands off a report and rarely sees what happens next. Real influence over remediation is much harder from outside the org, however good the report.
feedback.freelance: Freelance sits closer to agency here — a single retainer client gives you more continuity than a one-off agency engagement, but you're still outside the org's own prioritisation process most of the time.

contentSections.concept: **Continuity is the axis most people underweight when comparing routes.** In-house trades variety for the ability to see a fix through. Agency and freelance trade that continuity for breadth — seeing many products, many teams, many failure patterns, faster than an in-house role ever will.

contentSections.body:
Three dimensions worth being honest about, beyond the obvious pay-and-benefits comparison:

| | **In-house** | **Agency** | **Freelance** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pace** | Steady, sprint-cadence | Fast, deadline-driven, back-to-back engagements | Set by you, but income follows pace |
| **Autonomy over schedule** | Lowest — team hours, team meetings | Low-medium — client deadlines, utilisation targets | Highest, in theory |
| **Benefits & PTO** | Full, usually including accrued sick leave | Full, usually | None by default — self-funded |

The honest caveat on freelance autonomy: theoretical control over your schedule is only real if your income can survive you exercising it. A freelancer with one client and a thin buffer has less real autonomy than an in-house employee with generous accrued leave, even though the freelancer's calendar looks emptier on paper.
Compare routes on continuity, pace and *real* (not theoretical) autonomy — not just the salary line.

title: Adjacent roles this skill opens
description: The audit skill doesn't only lead to more auditing — it's the core of several other roles, each asking for a narrower slice of it.

learningObjectives.text: Identify roles adjacent to accessibility QA and which slice of the core skill each draws on
Assess which adjacent role fits a given background

contentSections.title: The skill is narrower than the job titles suggest

contentSections.body: "Accessibility QA" sounds like one job. It is closer to a base skill — telling a real barrier from a technical violation, and knowing which method would actually catch it — that at least six different job titles are built on top of, each keeping most of the skill and adding one specific thing.

Six roles worth knowing about, roughly in order of how directly they reuse the core audit skill:

1. **Accessibility QA / test automation engineer** — writes and maintains automated checks (axe-core, Playwright integrations) and knows exactly what they can and can't catch. Closest adjacent role to auditing itself.
2. **Accessibility program manager** — doesn't personally audit as much, but translates findings into a roadmap, tracks remediation, and negotiates between engineering, design and leadership.
3. **Accessibility-focused UX researcher** — runs and interprets sessions with disabled users; needs the audit skill's judgement about what's a barrier versus a preference, plus research methodology on top.
4. **Procurement / vendor accessibility reviewer** — reads VPATs and Accessibility Conformance Reports against what a real audit would find, catching vendors who filled in a template without testing anything.
5. **Accessibility trainer / developer advocate** — teaches the judgement, rather than applying it directly; needs to be able to explain *why*, not just flag *what*.
6. **Content designer with accessibility focus** — applies the same task-first thinking to plain language, error messages and reading level rather than markup.

contentSections.question: A QA automation engineer with two years of Selenium/Playwright experience wants to specialise. Order these next steps from lowest to highest commitment.
steps: Add axe-core scans to an existing test suite and learn to triage its output
Take on a manual keyboard-only pass on one product journey, alongside the automated work
Ask to shadow or assist on one full manual audit with a senior reviewer
Propose owning accessibility test strategy for the team as a defined part of the role
contentSections.explanation: This is a realistic on-ramp precisely because it never asks the person to stop being a QA engineer and become something else overnight. Each step keeps the paycheck and job title stable while adding one skill at a time — which matters enormously for someone who can't afford the income gap of a full career change, and is also just how skill actually accumulates.

contentSections.body: Most of these roles want 80% of what you already have from a QA or adjacent background, plus one specific addition — not a from-scratch career change.

contentSections.title: Choosing which door to walk through

contentSections.body: Two candidates read the same list of six roles. One has three years of manual QA and wants stability; the other has a research background and wants to work directly with disabled users. The list doesn't tell either of them which door to choose — their existing skills and what they want more of does.

contentSections.scenario: A content designer at a fintech company, currently writing microcopy and error messages, is considering a pivot into accessibility-focused content design.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine points in favour of that specific pivot for this specific person?

items.label: Error-message clarity is already core to their current job
They already write for a regulated industry where clarity has legal weight (financial disclosures, consent language)
Accessibility content design pays roughly the same as general content design at their level, so there's no real career cost to trying
Fintech is a sector with real, dated regulatory obligations, giving the pivot a fundable business case

explanation.a: Genuinely applicable — this is the closest possible match between an existing skill and the adjacent role's core work.
explanation.b: Genuinely applicable — writing under legal weight is a transferable habit that maps directly onto writing error messages that must be both clear and accurate.
explanation.c: Not something you can assert without checking — accessibility specialisation sometimes pays a premium and sometimes doesn't, depending on the org and market, and treating "probably fine" as evidence is the exact optimism this lesson is trying to head off.
explanation.d: Genuinely applicable — this is the same funding logic from lesson one, applied to a content role rather than a QA role.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the four are real, specific reasons this pivot fits this person. The one to distrust is the comfortable assumption dressed up as a fact — "probably pays about the same" is exactly the kind of claim to verify with real postings and real conversations before betting a career move on it, not something to wave through because it's convenient to believe.

contentSections.question: Guess first: of the six adjacent roles listed in this lesson, which one requires the *least* additional formal training on top of an existing QA background?
contentSections.answer: Accessibility QA / test automation engineer — it's a superset of the QA skills someone likely already has, plus the specific knowledge of what a scanner can and can't catch, which this whole module has been building toward directly.
contentSections.hint: Look for the role that's furthest down the "same skill, narrower slice" list from the start of this lesson.

contentSections.body: Choose the adjacent role that keeps the most of what you already do well, and verify the assumptions that feel too comfortable to check.

title: Rates and salaries, stated honestly
description: Real, honestly-caveated numbers for salaried and freelance accessibility work, and how to price an audit instead of guessing.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate salary and rate ranges against role type, seniority and region

contentSections.title: Numbers, with the caveats that make them usable

contentSections.body: A number given without its caveats is worse than no number at all — it lets someone anchor on a figure that has nothing to do with their actual market, region or scope.

Rough US-market figures, current as of the last few years, moving over time and varying a great deal by region and company size:

- **In-house accessibility specialist/QA:** roughly \$70k–\$130k salaried, with the wide range mostly explained by seniority and whether the role is individual-contributor or leads a program.
- **Consultancy/agency reviewer:** often salaried similarly to in-house at the junior-to-mid level, sometimes with billable-hour bonuses.
- **Freelance/independent audit work:** commonly billed \$75–\$200+/hour depending on experience, specialisation (screen reader testing specifically often commands more) and how the client found you — direct relationships typically pay better than marketplace platforms, which take a cut and drive rates down.

The honest caveat that applies to all three: these are US figures, and role titles are not standardised — "accessibility specialist" at one company is a QA role, at another is closer to a program manager, and the pay follows the actual scope, not the title.

contentSections.code:
Freelance quote to client:

"Full accessibility audit of your website: \$500 flat."
contentSections.question: What's the biggest problem with this quote, independent of whether \$500 is too low?

options.label: It doesn't name what "full" and "your website" actually cover
\$500 is definitely too low for any audit
It should be billed hourly instead

feedback.scope: Right — this is the same scoping failure from earlier in this module, in a pricing context. "Full" and "your website" aren't a scope; they're an invitation for the client to expect everything and for the reviewer to have quoted for something much smaller.
feedback.toolow: \$500 could be entirely fair for a five-page marketing site with an automated-plus-quick-manual pass, and badly underpriced for a forty-journey e-commerce platform. The number alone can't be judged as too low or too high without knowing the scope — which is exactly the missing piece.
feedback.hourly: Hourly isn't automatically the fix, as covered earlier — it just moves the risk instead of removing it. The actual fix here is naming the scope, regardless of which pricing model gets used on top of it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Full accessibility audit of your website" describes nothing checkable: not which pages, not which methods, not what happens if the client's site turns out to be four times the size the reviewer assumed. A defensible quote names journeys or page templates, methods (automated / manual / assistive-technology testing), and what's explicitly excluded.

contentSections.body: A rate or salary number is only as useful as the scope it's attached to — quote against journeys and methods, never against "the whole thing."

A freelancer pricing purely by estimated hours is pricing as if every week will be a good week. For someone with a chronic condition, that assumption is the thing most likely to make the business unsustainable within a year — which is exactly what module four of this phase covers in depth.

contentSections.scenario:
Two ways of building in a buffer for a scoped audit.

**A.** Quietly pad the hourly estimate by 30% so a bad week doesn't blow the budget, and say nothing about it.

**B.** Quote a flat fee tied to four named deliverable stages, with payment released as each stage completes — regardless of which calendar day that happens on.
contentSections.question: Which actually protects the reviewer on a genuinely bad week, without damaging trust with the client?

options.label: A — padding the estimate
B — staged flat fee

feedback.a: Padding works only until a client compares your estimate to a competitor's and it looks inflated — and it still leaves you exposed if the bad week is worse than the padding covers.
feedback.b: Right. A stage doesn't care which day it was finished on, so a lost week costs time, not money — and the client sees exactly what they're paying for at each stage, which builds trust instead of eroding it.

contentSections.concept: **Price in a buffer, don't hide it in the estimate.** State a stage-based flat fee tied to deliverables, not calendar days, and ask for payment released per stage rather than a single sum on final delivery. This is the same idea as staging an audit into resumable pieces, applied to money instead of time.

contentSections.question: Guess first: what's the main risk of billing hourly instead of by staged deliverable, specifically for someone with a variable-energy condition?
contentSections.answer: It ties income directly to hours actually logged — so a flare week isn't just a hard week, it's a pay cut on top of it. Staged flat pricing decouples the two.
contentSections.hint: Ask what happens to the invoice, not just the schedule, when a bad week hits.

contentSections.body: Price against deliverable stages, not calendar time — it protects both sides when the pace of the work is genuinely variable.

title: Remote and async-friendly employers
description: Telling a genuinely remote, async-friendly employer from a job posting that uses the word "remote" and means something else entirely.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish genuine remote/async culture from posting language that only claims it

contentSections.title: "Remote" is a word, not a culture

contentSections.body: A posting says "remote" three times. The interview process is four consecutive live video calls scheduled across nine days with no async option. By the third call it's clear which of the two claims — the word or the process — was telling the truth.

The interview process is the single best preview available before accepting an offer, because it's the part of the company's process you actually experience firsthand rather than reading about. Concrete things to notice:

- Is there any async or take-home component, or is everything a live call?
- When you ask about typical meeting load, does the answer include specific numbers, or just "we try to keep it light"?
- Are interview times offered across a real timezone range, or only during one region's business hours regardless of the role being advertised as global?
- Does anyone mention how the team documents decisions — written RFCs, recorded standups — or does everything sound like it lives in someone's head?

contentSections.intro: Build a short async-culture check from the pieces below — the questions worth actually asking in an interview, not just noticing passively.

options: "Do you like meetings?"
"Roughly how many hours a week are recurring meetings for someone in this role?"
"Is the team friendly?"
fields.correctValue: "Roughly how many hours a week are recurring meetings for someone in this role?"
fields.feedback: A specific number is answerable and checkable later; "do you like meetings" invites a socially safe non-answer.

options: "Are you a collaborative team?"
"If I joined and had a rough week, how would I catch up on what I missed?"
"Do you use Slack?"
fields.correctValue: "If I joined and had a rough week, how would I catch up on what I missed?"
fields.feedback: This directly tests whether async documentation is real practice or aspiration, and it's a question a genuinely async team can answer specifically and quickly.

options: "Is the role remote?"
"What hours does the team consider core overlap, and how strict is that?"
"Do you have an office?"
fields.correctValue: "What hours does the team consider core overlap, and how strict is that?"
fields.feedback: "Is it remote" is already answered by the posting. The overlap window and how strictly it's enforced is the actual operating detail that determines whether the role fits a variable schedule.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these three questions are confrontational or unusual to ask in an interview — they're exactly the kind of specific, practical questions a genuinely async-friendly employer will be glad to answer clearly, because they've thought about the answer before. A vague or defensive response to any of them is itself useful data.

contentSections.body: Ask specific, checkable questions about meetings, documentation and overlap hours — the answers tell you more than the word "remote" ever will.
A search that only reads job postings is reading the least reliable source available. Three better ones exist, each harder to fake than the last.

contentSections.scenario: A company scores well on a public disability-inclusion index company-wide, but a candidate interviewing for one specific team hears nothing but live, back-to-back calls throughout the process, with no async option offered.
contentSections.question: What's the most defensible read of this mismatch?

options.label: The index must be fake
A company-wide score doesn't guarantee every individual team runs the same way
The candidate is overreacting to a normal interview process

feedback.fake: Indices like this are audited at the organisation level and are generally real — the mismatch is more simply explained by scope than by fraud.
feedback.team: Right. A company-wide index score is evidence about the organisation, not a guarantee about the one team a candidate would actually join — the interview process for that specific team is still the higher-resolution signal.
feedback.overreact: The interview process is real, first-hand evidence about how this specific team works, not an overreaction — treating it as noise throws away the most direct signal available.

contentSections.mechanism: Every signal in this lesson is evidence to weigh at a different resolution — sector-wide, company-wide, or team-specific — and the team-specific signal (the actual interview process) should generally outweigh a broader one when they conflict, because it's the one that predicts what the candidate's actual daily experience will be.

contentSections.body:
A few concrete places this search differs from a general job hunt:

- **Sector matters as much as posting language.** Developer-tools companies, open-source-adjacent businesses and distributed-first startups (companies that were remote before it was common) tend to have genuinely mature async practice, because they had to build it before it was fashionable to claim.
- **Disability-inclusive employer indices exist and are checkable**, such as the US Disability Equality Index (jointly run by Disability:IN and the American Association of People with Disabilities) — a public score, not a self-description, which makes it harder to fake than a careers-page paragraph.
- **Current employees are the highest-signal source available before you apply.** A search for people who hold the exact role you're considering, at that exact company, posting publicly about their actual day-to-day, beats any amount of careers-page copy.

contentSections.question: Guess first: which single source in this lesson is hardest for a company to fake convincingly?
contentSections.answer: A current employee in the exact role, posting publicly and specifically about their actual day-to-day — it's first-hand, detailed, and costs the company nothing to produce, which is exactly why it can't be manufactured the way a careers page can.
contentSections.hint: Rank the four sources — posting language, sector, public index, employee testimony — by how much effort a company would need to fabricate each one convincingly.

contentSections.body: Look past the posting to the sector, a public disability-inclusion index, and current employees' own accounts — each one is harder to fake than the posting's own language, and the most specific signal should outweigh the broadest one.

Whichever of these needed a hint is worth a second look before the checkpoint — that's the point of the set.

title: Lab — Research and Document Your Target Market
description: Produce a market document naming ten real employers across your target routes and what each actually screens for — the document you'll keep returning to across your job search.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's employer-category and remote-signal framework to real research
Produce a usable market document with prioritised, evidenced entries

contentSections.body: A market document isn't a wishlist — it's a working reference you'll reopen every time you're deciding where to spend a good week's job-search energy, so it needs to hold real evidence, not just names.

contentSections.title: Your target market document
contentSections.brief: You're about to spend real energy on a job search, and energy spent applying to the wrong ten employers is energy you don't get back. Before applying anywhere, build a document naming ten real employers you'd actually consider, across the routes this module covered, each with concrete evidence of what they screen for and how they operate — not a list of logos.
contentSections.deliverable: A market document listing ten real employers (a mix of in-house roles, agencies/consultancies, and potential freelance clients), each with: which of the five funding categories they fall into, what their postings and interview process actually reveal about pace and remote culture, and a rough sense of what they'd screen a candidate for.

stages.title: Set your screening criteria first
stages.instructions: Before researching anyone, write down what actually matters to you across the dimensions this module covered: route (in-house/agency/freelance), pace, remote/async reality, and pay range. Rank your top three. This step exists so the research that follows is filtered by your real constraints, not just by who happens to be hiring.
stages.checkpoint: You have three ranked criteria, specific enough that a real posting could be checked against them.

stages.title: Research ten real employers
stages.instructions: Find ten real organisations — a mix across in-house, agency and potential freelance clients — that plausibly fund accessibility work. For each, note: which funding category it falls into (from lesson one), what its postings or public materials reveal about remote/async culture (from lesson five), and any adjacent-role opening it might have beyond a straight audit title (from lesson three). Use real organisations you could name to someone else, not placeholders.
stages.checkpoint: You have ten named, real entries, each with at least the funding category and one concrete culture signal.

stages.title: Prioritise and write the summary
stages.instructions: Rank your ten against the criteria from stage one. Write a two-to-three sentence summary for your top three explaining specifically why they rank there — not just "seems good," but the concrete evidence behind the ranking.
stages.checkpoint: Your top three each have a specific, evidenced reason for their ranking, not a vague impression.

rubric.criterion: Ten real, named employers
rubric.meets: Every entry is a real, specific organisation — not a category or a placeholder.

rubric.criterion: Funding category is identified for each
rubric.meets: Each entry names which of the five categories from lesson one applies, and why.

rubric.criterion: Remote/async evidence is concrete
rubric.meets: Signals cited are specific and checkable (posting language, interview structure, public employee accounts) — not just "says remote."

rubric.criterion: Prioritisation is evidenced, not vibes
rubric.meets: The top three each have a stated, specific reason tied back to your own criteria.

title: The certification landscape and what each signals
description: What CPACC, WAS, CPWA, Trusted Tester and vendor certificates each actually verify — and the gap between what a certificate signals and what a job requires.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish what each major accessibility credential actually verifies
Identify what a certification alone does not demonstrate

contentSections.body: Two candidates apply for the same audit role. One lists "IAAP CPACC" on their resume. The other lists nothing formal but describes three real audits in detail. The hiring manager who knows what CPACC actually tests reads these very differently than one who doesn't.

contentSections.scenario: Four real credentials in this space: **CPACC** (IAAP) is a knowledge exam on disability, accessibility principles and law. **WAS** (IAAP) tests hands-on technical evaluation skill against WCAG. **Trusted Tester** (US DHS) is a free, government-run program certifying a specific manual testing methodology, mainly used for federal work. **CPWA** is CPACC plus WAS combined.
contentSections.question: A candidate wants to prove they can technically audit a real product against WCAG. Which single credential is the closest match?

options.label: CPACC
WAS
Any of them equally

feedback.cpacc: CPACC verifies broad foundational knowledge — disability, principles, law — not hands-on technical audit skill against WCAG specifically.
feedback.was: Right. WAS is specifically the technical, hands-on evaluation credential in this set — the one that most directly maps to "can this person audit a real product."
feedback.any: They're not interchangeable — CPACC and WAS test genuinely different things, and treating them as equally relevant to a technical audit claim overstates what CPACC verifies.

contentSections.concept: **Read a credential's name and scope literally before citing it as proof of something it doesn't test.** CPACC is knowledge; WAS is skill; Trusted Tester is a specific government methodology; CPWA is both combined. None of the four verify that someone has actually shipped real audit work for a real client.

contentSections.body: The wider landscape beyond these four: Deque University offers paid, skill-specific certificates (e.g. web accessibility fundamentals) that are respected in the industry without being a formal professional credential; various free courses (edX, Coursera, W3C's own WAI curricula) build foundational knowledge without any certification at the end at all. None of these, including the four above, substitute for demonstrated work — they're evidence of study, not of judgment under real conditions.
Read what a credential's own scope actually claims — CPACC is knowledge, WAS is skill, Trusted Tester is a specific methodology, and none of them are a portfolio.

contentSections.title: What a certificate gets you, and what it doesn't

contentSections.body: A certificate gets a resume past an automated keyword filter and gives an interviewer a reason to ask a follow-up question. It has never, on its own, produced a good audit.

contentSections.scenario: An interviewer asks a CPACC-certified candidate to walk through how they'd prioritise two real findings from a mock audit. The candidate can name the relevant WCAG criteria for both but struggles to say which one actually blocks more users.
contentSections.question: What does this gap most likely indicate?

options.label: The candidate is lying about being certified
The certification tested knowledge that this specific judgment call — task impact over citation — was never part of
CPACC is a worthless credential

feedback.lying: Nothing here suggests dishonesty — the candidate can correctly name the criteria, which is exactly what CPACC tests. The gap is elsewhere.
feedback.scope: Right. This is precisely the foundations-phase distinction between citing a criterion and judging task impact — a knowledge exam like CPACC was never designed to test that judgment, which only comes from doing real audit work.
feedback.worthless: Not worthless — CPACC is real, useful evidence of foundational study. It's just evidence of a different thing than the judgment this interview question is testing.

contentSections.mechanism: A certification and a portfolio answer different interview questions. "Do you know the field's vocabulary and principles?" is answered by a credential. "Can you make a defensible prioritisation call on a real finding?" is only answered by having done it — which is exactly what the next lesson's proof strategy addresses directly.

contentSections.question: Guess first: for a career changer with zero accessibility work history, is a foundational certification like CPACC worth pursuing?
contentSections.answer: Often yes, specifically as a fast, low-cost signal of serious intent while a portfolio is being built — not as a substitute for the portfolio. The mistake is stopping there.
contentSections.hint: Weigh what it costs against what it credibly proves, for someone with literally nothing else to show yet.

contentSections.body: A certificate answers "do you know the field"; the job usually asks "can you make the call" — which only real work answers.

title: Cost, renewal and whether employers require it
description: What these credentials actually cost in money and upkeep, and how rarely they're a genuine hard requirement versus a stated preference.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate certification cost and renewal burden against likely return

contentSections.body: A certification's sticker price is the smallest number in the real cost. The recurring one — renewal fees, continuing-education hours, a re-exam every few years — is the number that determines whether it's worth pursuing on a fixed budget of energy and money.

contentSections.scenario: IAAP credentials (CPACC, WAS, CPWA) require ongoing IAAP membership plus periodic recertification through continuing education credits or re-examination, roughly every three years. Trusted Tester is free to obtain (a US government program) but requires periodic reassessment to stay current. Vendor certificates (like Deque University's) typically don't expire but also carry less standalone weight as a credential.
contentSections.question: For someone choosing based purely on lowest ongoing cost, which option fits best?

options.label: IAAP CPACC/WAS/CPWA
Trusted Tester
A non-expiring vendor certificate

feedback.iaap: IAAP credentials carry the highest ongoing cost of the three — membership plus recurring recertification.
feedback.tt: Right, on pure cost — free to obtain, government-run, though it does still require periodic reassessment to remain current, which costs time even at zero dollars.
feedback.vendor: Cheapest to maintain since it doesn't expire, but it's also the credential carrying the least standalone recognition outside contexts that specifically know the vendor.

contentSections.concept: **Cost and recognition move somewhat in opposite directions here**, and the honest trade-off is between a credential that costs more to maintain but carries broader recognition, and one that costs little but proves less to someone unfamiliar with it.

contentSections.body: On whether employers actually require it: genuinely mandatory certification requirements are uncommon outside one specific context — government contracts that name a required credential (usually Trusted Tester) as a literal deliverable condition, because a federal agency needs to show a specific methodology was used. Outside that context, "certification preferred" vastly outnumbers "certification required," and even postings using the word "required" are frequently negotiable in practice, as covered in the next exercise.
The recurring cost, not the sticker price, is what should drive the decision — and outside government contracting, "required" in a posting rarely means what it says.

contentSections.title: Deciding whether it's worth it for you, specifically

contentSections.body: The right answer to "should I get certified" depends entirely on what gap it's meant to close — and for most people at most career stages, that gap is better closed a different way.

contentSections.code:
Career plan:

"Step 1: Get IAAP CPACC and WAS.
Step 2: Apply to jobs.
Step 3: Get hired."
contentSections.question: What's missing from this plan that this whole phase has been building toward?

options.label: A timeline for each step
Any demonstrated, real work — a portfolio, contributions, or practice audits
A third credential

feedback.timeline: A timeline would help pace the plan, but it's not the structural gap — the plan could have perfect dates and still be missing the thing hiring managers actually screen for.
feedback.portfolio: Right. Two credentials without any demonstrated work is exactly the CPACC-only interview gap from the previous lesson, scaled up — the plan spends real time and money on the weaker form of proof and skips the stronger one entirely.
feedback.third: More credentials compound the same problem rather than solving it — the gap isn't credential count, it's the total absence of demonstrated work.

contentSections.flawExplanation: This plan treats certification as sufficient on its own, when it's most useful as a floor built alongside real demonstrated work, not a replacement for it — which is exactly what the rest of this module addresses.

contentSections.question: Guess first: for someone with 3+ years of hands-on accessibility QA experience already, is a first-time certification usually worth pursuing?
contentSections.answer: Often marginal — the portfolio and work history already do most of what a certification would signal, so the return is lower than for a career changer with nothing else to show yet.
contentSections.hint: Ask what specific gap the certification would close for someone who already has the harder-won evidence.

contentSections.body: Certification is worth the most to someone who has the least other proof yet — and worth progressively less as real work history accumulates.

title: Portfolio as the stronger proof
description: Turning real audit work into a portfolio piece that demonstrates judgment, not just that a defect was found — the strongest form of proof this field has.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a portfolio piece that demonstrates audit judgment rather than checklist completion
Evaluate which portfolio elements provide genuine evidence versus surface polish

contentSections.title: From a finding to a portfolio piece

contentSections.body: A raw finding says a defect exists. A portfolio piece has to do something a raw finding doesn't: show the reasoning that got from noticing the defect to deciding it mattered and knowing how to fix it well.

contentSections.problem: Turn this raw finding into a portfolio piece: "Modal dialog on a checkout page doesn't trap focus — tabbing moves behind the modal."

steps.label: State the task and impact
steps.work: A screen reader or keyboard user opening the shipping-address modal on this checkout flow can tab past its boundary into content behind it, losing track of whether the modal is even still open — and, on this specific implementation, landing back on page content with no clear way back into the modal without restarting the flow.
steps.why: Leads with what a person experiences, exactly like the foundations-phase finding structure — an interviewer skimming a portfolio should get the impact in one sentence.

steps.label: Show the specific mechanism
steps.work: The modal is a `<div role="dialog">` with no focus trap implemented — no listener catching Tab at the last focusable element to cycle it back to the first. `aria-modal="true"` is present, but that attribute is a hint to assistive technology; it does not enforce focus containment on its own.
steps.why: This is the detail that separates a portfolio piece from a bug report — it shows understanding of *why* the markup alone doesn't solve the problem, not just that something's broken.

steps.label: Explain the fix and the trade-off considered
steps.work: The fix adds a keydown listener on Tab and Shift+Tab at the dialog's first and last focusable elements, cycling focus back into the dialog, plus returning focus to the triggering button on close. The trade-off considered: a simpler `inert` attribute on the rest of the page was evaluated first, but browser support at the time made the manual listener the safer choice for this codebase's supported browser matrix.
steps.why: Naming an alternative you considered and rejected, with a reason, is strong evidence of judgment — it shows you didn't just apply the first fix you found.

faded.problem: Turn this raw finding into a portfolio piece: "Error summary at the top of a form isn't announced when it appears after a failed submit."

blanks.prompt: State the task and impact — what does a screen reader user experience?
blanks.answer: They submit the form, hear nothing change, and have no way to know the submission failed or why, unless they manually re-navigate to the top of the page to discover the error summary.
accept: they get no indication the submission failed
no announcement of the new error summary
blanks.why: Leads with the blocked task, not the technical cause.

blanks.prompt: Show the specific mechanism — why doesn't this announce automatically?
blanks.answer: The error summary is inserted into the DOM without being placed in a live region and without focus being moved to it, so assistive technology has no signal that new, important content just appeared.
accept: focus isn't moved to the new content
blanks.why: This is the technical judgment a portfolio reader is actually evaluating.

blanks.prompt: Explain a fix and a trade-off you'd consider
blanks.answer: Move focus to the error summary on failed submit (e.g. a heading with tabindex="-1"), which announces reliably and also gives keyboard users a clear starting point — considered over a plain live region alone, which announces but doesn't help a keyboard user locate the summary visually afterward.
accept: focus management plus optional live region
blanks.why: Naming the alternative and why it's weaker is the judgment signal.

contentSections.procedure: Task-and-impact first, mechanism second, fix-with-a-considered-alternative third. Every strong portfolio piece in this field follows roughly this shape.

contentSections.body: A portfolio piece earns its keep by showing the reasoning between the finding and the fix — not just that either one exists.

contentSections.title: What actually counts as evidence, and what's just polish

contentSections.body: Two portfolio pages can look equally professional and carry very different amounts of real evidence — polish is easy to produce and easy to overweight when reviewing your own work.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate's portfolio page includes several elements.
contentSections.question: Which of these are genuine evidence of audit judgment, versus surface polish that doesn't actually demonstrate it?

items.label: A before/after case study with a stated trade-off, as built in this lesson
A polished visual design for the portfolio site itself
A recorded screen reader walkthrough showing an actual barrier, narrated
A long list of WCAG success criteria definitions copied from the spec
A dated, maintainer-approved open-source contribution linked directly

explanation.a: Real evidence — shows the specific reasoning this whole lesson has been building toward.
explanation.b: Visual polish is worth having, but it's evidence of design skill, not audit judgment — don't let it substitute for the substance underneath it.
explanation.c: Real evidence — a genuine, narrated barrier discovery in real time is very hard to fake and shows fluency directly.
explanation.d: This is closer to a study aid than a portfolio piece — copying spec definitions demonstrates access to the spec, not judgment about applying it.
explanation.e: Real, externally-verified evidence — a maintainer's approval is a second party vouching for the work, which is stronger than any self-reported claim.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern across the genuine-evidence items: each one shows reasoning or is externally verified. The polish and copied-content items are easy to produce and easy to mistake for substance, especially when reviewing your own portfolio — a useful discipline is asking of every item, "does this show a decision I made, or just that I have access to information?"

contentSections.question: Guess first: how many strong portfolio pieces (in this lesson's sense) does it typically take to change how a candidate is read in an interview?
contentSections.answer: Often as few as two or three well-reasoned pieces, if each genuinely shows judgment — quality and reasoning depth matter far more here than volume.
contentSections.hint: Think about how the worked example above would land if a hiring manager saw just one, done that thoroughly.

contentSections.body: Ask of every portfolio item: does this show a decision I made, or just that I have access to information? Keep the former, cut the latter.

title: Publishing an audit of a public site, ethically
description: The consent and anonymisation questions to settle before publishing real audit work, so a portfolio piece never becomes an unconsented public callout.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate the ethical soundness of a plan to publish real audit work

contentSections.title: Whose work is it to publish?

contentSections.body: Doing the audit and having the right to publish specifics about it in public are two separate questions, and conflating them is the single most common mistake people make with their first case-study post.

contentSections.scenario: Four possible sources for a published case study: **(1)** a paid client engagement, no explicit publishing agreement in the contract; **(2)** a personal practice audit of your own side project; **(3)** an open-source project's public issue tracker; **(4)** a public government website's accessibility statement page.
contentSections.question: Which of these can generally be published from directly, without seeking separate consent first?

options.label: Only (1)
(2), (3) and (4) — not (1) without asking
All four equally

feedback.one: Backwards — (1) is exactly the one that needs separate consent, since it's someone else's product and the contract didn't grant publishing rights.
feedback.rest: Right. Your own project needs no one else's consent; open-source issue trackers are already public and built for exactly this kind of discussion; and government sites are public-facing and, in many jurisdictions, actively invite accessibility feedback.
feedback.all: Not all four — a paid client engagement without an explicit publishing agreement is a genuinely different case and needs consent first, regardless of how the other three are treated.

contentSections.concept: **A contract to do audit work is not automatically a license to publish about it.** Publishing rights are a separate, explicit thing to secure — either in the original agreement or by asking afterward — and the safest default sources for a first case study are your own work, open-source projects, and public-sector sites, precisely because consent is either unnecessary or already built into the context.

contentSections.body: A useful middle path when a client engagement is genuinely your best material and direct consent isn't available: anonymise thoroughly. Change the sector detail, remove any identifying screenshot content, describe the pattern rather than the specific product. Done well, this teaches the method just as effectively as naming the client would, without the risk.
Own work, open-source, and public-sector sites are the safest defaults; anything else needs explicit consent or real anonymisation first.

contentSections.title: When a post reads as a callout, whatever the intent

contentSections.body: Intent doesn't control how a post reads. A post titled with a real company's name next to a list of its failures reads as a callout to that company's customers and staff, regardless of whether the author meant it as constructive.

contentSections.code:
Blog post title:

"5 Accessibility Failures at [Real Local Bakery]'s Online Ordering Page"

(with screenshots, no prior contact with the business)
contentSections.question: What's the core problem, independent of whether the findings are accurate?

options.label: It names and publicly criticises a real, small, identifiable business with no notice or consent
Blog posts about real companies are never appropriate
The findings are probably wrong

feedback.names: Right — this is the exact pattern flagged earlier in this lesson: doing the work doesn't create a right to publish specifics about someone else's product, and a small business has far less capacity to absorb public criticism than a large company would.
feedback.never: Too strong — large, well-resourced companies are written about publicly all the time, including critically, as part of normal industry discourse. The specific problem here is the combination of a small, identifiable target and zero prior contact.
feedback.wrong: Accuracy isn't the issue this exercise is testing — the problem holds even if every finding is completely correct.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isn't necessarily "never publish this" — it's contact the business first and offer the findings directly, or anonymise the post so the specific bakery can't be identified, preserving the teaching value without the public-callout risk to a small business that never agreed to be featured.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does this ethical caution scale down for a large, well-resourced company rather than a small local business?
contentSections.answer: Generally yes, somewhat — a large company has more capacity to absorb public critique and is already the subject of far more public commentary. But consent and accuracy still matter; "large enough to handle it" isn't a blank check.
contentSections.hint: Think about the difference in real-world consequence between naming a Fortune 500 company's known public failure versus naming a five-person local business.

contentSections.body: If a post would read as a callout to someone who never agreed to be featured, that's the signal to anonymise or ask first — not a detail to hope nobody notices.

title: Contributing to open-source accessibility work
description: Where a first open-source accessibility contribution realistically starts, and how to make one that's visible, dated and genuinely useful to a portfolio.

learningObjectives.text: Apply a realistic path to a first open-source accessibility contribution

contentSections.body: "Contribute to open source" sounds like it means submitting a pull request to a major project on day one. For almost everyone, the realistic starting point is much smaller and much less intimidating than that.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a realistic first-contribution plan from the choices below.

options: A random, unfamiliar large codebase
A project with an active accessibility label, or a component library's 'good first issue' tag
Only the very newest, least-maintained repos
fields.correctValue: A project with an active accessibility label, or a component library's 'good first issue' tag
fields.feedback: Active labels mean a maintainer is already engaged with accessibility work and likely to review a contribution — projects like axe-core, the W3C's ARIA Authoring Practices Guide repo, and popular component libraries (Radix, react-aria, Material UI) all label issues this way.

fields.prompt: What to submit first, if code isn't ready yet
options: Nothing — wait until fully confident writing code
A clearly-written issue report on a real barrier you found
A pull request without reading the contribution guide
fields.correctValue: A clearly-written issue report on a real barrier you found
fields.feedback: A well-written issue is a complete, legitimate contribution on its own — many maintainers value a precise bug report as much as a fix, especially from someone establishing trust with the project.

fields.prompt: What kind of task fits a lower-energy day
options: A deep debugging session in unfamiliar code
A documentation fix or a clarifying comment on an existing issue
Nothing — save all open-source work for high-energy days only
fields.correctValue: A documentation fix or a clarifying comment on an existing issue
fields.feedback: Documentation and discussion contributions require careful reading and clear writing, not sustained debugging focus — a genuinely different, and often more accessible, kind of task.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these choices require code fluency as a prerequisite, and that's the point: a realistic first contribution meets you at whatever energy and skill level a given week actually offers, and every level of it builds the same visible, dated history.

contentSections.body: Start with an active label and a clearly-written issue if code isn't ready — a documentation fix on a low-energy day counts just as much as a merged pull request.

contentSections.title: Why this matters for a portfolio specifically

contentSections.body: A dated, public, maintainer-approved contribution has one property no self-published portfolio piece can match on its own: someone else, with no reason to be generous, looked at the work and accepted it.

contentSections.scenario: Two portfolio items: a self-written case study, and a merged pull request fixing a missing accessible name on a component library's button, with a maintainer's approving review visible in the public history.
contentSections.question: Why does the merged pull request often carry more weight with a skeptical reviewer, beyond just being real work?

options.label: Code is inherently more impressive than writing
It's independently verified — a third party with no stake in the candidate's success reviewed and accepted it
Open-source work is always paid, so it proves professionalism

feedback.code: Not the reason — a well-reasoned case study can be just as impressive as a small code fix, and this module has spent real time establishing that writing-based portfolio pieces are legitimate evidence too.
feedback.verified: Right. Third-party verification, from someone with no incentive to be kind, is a categorically different kind of evidence than anything self-published — it's the open-source equivalent of the maintainer-approved evidence highlighted earlier in this module.
feedback.paid: Most open-source contribution is unpaid — that's not the mechanism making it strong evidence here.

contentSections.mechanism: Self-published work proves you can produce something that looks right. Third-party-reviewed work proves someone else, independently, agreed it was right — which is a meaningfully stronger claim, and worth pursuing specifically because of that difference.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it worth pursuing open-source contributions even if you already have several strong self-published case studies?
contentSections.answer: Yes — they're complementary, not redundant. Self-published work shows your own reasoning in full; third-party-verified work shows someone else agreed, which a self-published piece structurally can't demonstrate on its own.
contentSections.hint: Ask whether the two kinds of evidence answer the exact same question, or two different ones.

contentSections.body: Third-party review is evidence a self-published portfolio piece can't produce on its own — worth pursuing alongside your case studies, not instead of them.

title: Lab — Publish One Public Work Sample
description: Produce and publish one real piece of proof — an audit case study or an open-source contribution — with the ethics of publishing it deliberately considered rather than assumed.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's portfolio and publishing-ethics standards to a real, published piece of work
Produce a public work sample with its scope and consent basis stated explicitly

contentSections.body: Everything in this module is preparation for one act: putting something real and public into the world that someone else can evaluate. This lab is that act, not a simulation of it.

contentSections.title: Your published work sample
contentSections.brief: Produce one real, public piece of proof: either a case study of a real audit finding (from your own work, consented client work, or a personal practice project) or an open-source accessibility contribution (an issue, a documentation fix, or a code fix). Whichever you choose, the ethics of publishing it need to be settled and stated, not assumed.
contentSections.deliverable: One published artefact (a blog post, a public repo write-up, or a merged/submitted open-source contribution), plus a short written note stating its source, consent basis and, if applicable, anonymisation choices.

stages.title: Choose your source and settle consent
stages.instructions: Decide which route you're taking — a case study from your own or consented work, or an open-source contribution — using lesson four's framework. If it involves anyone else's product, name explicitly how consent or anonymisation is handled before you write a word.
stages.checkpoint: You can state in one sentence why this specific source needs no further consent, or what consent/anonymisation step you've taken.

stages.title: Produce the artefact
stages.instructions: Write the case study using the task-impact-mechanism-fix structure from lesson three, or make the open-source contribution using the realistic starting point from lesson five (an issue report is a complete, valid choice if a code fix isn't realistic this week).
stages.checkpoint: You have a complete draft or a submitted contribution, not a partial start.

stages.title: Publish and self-check
stages.instructions: Publish it publicly (post it, submit the PR/issue, or push it live) and write the short consent/ethics note required by the deliverable. Then self-check against the rubric below before considering the lab done.
stages.checkpoint: The work is live and publicly visible, with the ethics note attached.

rubric.criterion: The source and consent basis are explicit
rubric.meets: A reader can tell exactly where the material came from and why publishing it is ethically sound, without guessing.

rubric.criterion: It demonstrates judgment, not just a finding
rubric.meets: The reasoning behind a decision — a fix trade-off, a prioritisation call, a contribution choice — is visible, not just the outcome.

rubric.criterion: It's actually public
rubric.meets: The artefact is live and reachable by someone else, not sitting in a private draft.

rubric.criterion: Nobody was named or exposed without agreement
rubric.meets: Any real person or organisation referenced either consented or can't be identified from what's published.

contentSections.body: This is the piece you'll point to the next time someone asks "what can you actually show me" — worth doing once, properly, rather than starting three and finishing none.
