title: The take-home audit task and how it's marked
description: What a typical take-home audit assignment actually asks for, and what separates a submission that gets marked well from one that doesn't — usually judgment, not coverage.

learningObjectives.text: Analyse what a take-home audit task is actually screening for
Apply staged-scope judgment to a time-boxed take-home assignment

contentSections.title: What the task is actually testing

contentSections.body: Two candidates get the identical take-home: audit a signup form, four hours, no further instructions. One submits nineteen findings. The other submits six. The one with six gets the offer.

contentSections.scenario: The nineteen-finding submission is mostly a re-formatted automated scan export, sorted by WCAG success criterion number, with brief one-line descriptions. The six-finding submission is a prioritised list, each with task impact stated first, severity reasoning, and one alternative fix considered and rejected for two of them.
contentSections.question: Why does the shorter submission read as stronger, given this track's whole approach so far?

options.label: Shorter submissions are always preferred regardless of content
It demonstrates the actual skill being screened for — prioritisation and reasoning — rather than tool output
Nineteen findings is simply too many to be believable

feedback.shorter: Length itself isn't the variable — a thorough, well-reasoned twelve-finding submission would read just as well. What matters is what's behind the numbers.
feedback.judgment: Right. A take-home is a proxy for real audit work, and real audit work is judged on whether findings are prioritised and defensible, not on raw count — which is exactly the distinction the foundations phase built between a violation list and a task-impact report.
feedback.toomany: Nineteen findings on a signup form isn't implausible on its own — the problem is what those findings actually are (largely raw scan output) and how they're presented, not the count.

contentSections.concept: **A take-home task is a compressed proxy for the actual job, and it's marked the way the actual job is judged** — on whether findings are prioritised by impact and reasoned through, not on how many were produced or how exhaustively a tool's output was transcribed.

contentSections.body: Concrete markers of a strong submission, almost always present in a rubric even when the candidate never sees it: findings framed around task impact before citation; explicit severity reasoning, not just a label; at least one finding that required genuine judgment rather than being obvious from a scan; and — when scope clearly exceeds the time given — an honest statement of what wasn't covered, echoing the staged-audit habit from earlier in this track.
A take-home is judged on prioritisation and reasoning, not on how much of a scanner's output got transcribed into a document.

contentSections.title: When the scope is bigger than the time

contentSections.body: Most take-home tasks are deliberately, or accidentally, more scope than the stated time genuinely allows — which is itself part of what's being tested.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate is given ninety minutes to audit a five-page, multi-step checkout flow.
contentSections.question: Roughly what share of candidates, in this scenario, submit work covering all five pages rather than stating an honest, narrower scope?
contentSections.explanation: Most candidates try to cover everything and end up either rushing every page shallowly or running out of time mid-task with no clear summary — the honest-scope response covered in this lesson is the less common choice, which is exactly why it stands out to a marker who has seen the pattern many times.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is submitting less scope, stated honestly, ever actually the wrong call on a take-home?
contentSections.answer: Rarely, if the scope narrowing is explicit and the reasoning for what was prioritised is stated — the risk is only real if the narrowing looks like an oversight rather than a deliberate choice.
contentSections.hint: Think about what distinguishes a deliberate, stated scope decision from simply running out of time silently.

contentSections.body: When the task gives you more scope than time, narrow it deliberately and say so — that's the same judgment a real engagement requires, tested under a clock.

title: Talking through an audit out loud
description: Narrating a live, observed audit under interview pressure — what to say when you're confident, and exactly what to say when you're not.

learningObjectives.text: Construct clear, honest narration for a live audit interview

contentSections.title: Narrating the reasoning, not just the result

contentSections.body: A candidate audits a page in total silence for six minutes, then announces four findings. The interviewer learns almost nothing about how those four findings were reached — which was the entire point of asking for a live exercise instead of another take-home.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways of narrating the same moment in a live audit: **A.** "This button has no accessible name." **B.** "I'm checking this button's accessible name — the visible label is an icon with no text, and I don't see an aria-label in the markup, so a screen reader would likely announce this as just 'button,' with no way to tell what it does."
contentSections.question: Which version does the actual job of a live interview exercise?

options.label: A
B

feedback.a: This states a conclusion without showing the checking process — an interviewer watching this learns the candidate can spot a known pattern, but nothing about how they got there.
feedback.b: Right. This narrates what's being checked, what's found, and why it matters — which is what a live exercise exists to surface that a written take-home can't.

contentSections.concept: **Narrate the checking, not just the conclusion.** State what you're looking at, what you're checking for and why, then the finding — every step, out loud, even the ones that turn out fine.

contentSections.body: Narrate the process, not just the conclusions — the process is what a live exercise is actually for.
Every live audit interview eventually hits something the candidate doesn't immediately recognise. What happens in the next ten seconds matters more than almost anything else in the exercise.

contentSections.code:
Interview transcript excerpt:

Candidate: "Yeah, um, this is probably fine, I think... it's probably okay, let's move on."
contentSections.question: What's the core problem with this response to an unfamiliar element?

options.label: It's too short
It states an unverified guess as a soft conclusion instead of naming the actual uncertainty
It should have included a WCAG citation

feedback.short: Length isn't the issue — a short, honest "I'm not sure, let me check" would be a strong response.
feedback.guess: Right. "Probably fine" dressed up as a soft verdict is worse than either a confident wrong answer or an honest "I don't know" — it neither commits to a checkable claim nor names the actual gap in knowledge.
feedback.citation: A citation wouldn't fix the underlying problem — the issue is the guess being presented as a conclusion, not a missing reference.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix is specific and checkable uncertainty: "I'm not sure whether this passes — let me actually test it with the keyboard before I call it either way," which is exactly the move built in exercise AQA-CR3-002.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does pausing silently for a few seconds to think, before speaking, hurt a candidate in this kind of interview?
contentSections.answer: Generally no — a short, visible thinking pause reads as normal and even reassuring. What hurts is an unexplained long silence with no narration at all, or a confident guess presented as fact.
contentSections.hint: Distinguish a pause with intent to speak next from silence that leaves the interviewer with nothing to evaluate.

contentSections.body: A confident guess dressed as a conclusion is worse than an honest, specific 'I'm not sure — let me check.' Say the uncertainty out loud.

title: Questions about disagreement and severity
description: Defending a severity call under pushback without either capitulating instantly or refusing to update — the judgment interviewers most often test directly.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate how to respond to pushback on a severity rating without new evidence
Distinguish appropriate flexibility from unfounded concession under social pressure

contentSections.title: The scenario almost every hiring process includes

contentSections.body: "The engineering lead disagrees with your High severity rating and wants it downgraded to Medium so it doesn't block the sprint. What do you do?" is close to the single most common interview question in this field, because it's the single most common real situation.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate, asked this exact question, answers: "I'd probably just go with Medium — I don't want to hold up the team over a disagreement."
contentSections.question: What does this answer most likely signal to the interviewer?

options.label: Strong collaborative instincts
A rating that folds under social pressure with no new evidence, which undermines the whole point of an independent audit
Good time management

feedback.collab: Collaboration matters, but this specific answer collapses the rating for social comfort rather than genuine new information — that's not collaboration, it's the audit's independence quietly disappearing under pressure.
feedback.folds: Right. If a severity rating changes the instant someone with more organisational power objects, with no new evidence offered, the rating was never really independent — which defeats much of the reason an outside or objective reviewer was brought in.
feedback.time: Nothing about this answer relates to time management — the issue is what the concession reveals about how the rating was arrived at in the first place.

contentSections.mechanism: An interviewer asking this question is testing whether a candidate's judgment holds up against organisational pressure, because that's exactly the pressure a real hire will face on day one — softening a legitimate finding to avoid friction is one of the most common ways good audit work gets quietly diluted inside an organisation.

contentSections.body: A rating that changes under pressure with no new evidence was never independent — the response should defend the reasoning or ask what new information the pushback is based on.
The failure mode on the other side is just as real: a reviewer who treats every pushback as an attack and refuses to update a rating even when the pushback surfaces a genuine new fact.

contentSections.scenario: An engineering lead pushes back on a High severity rating for a keyboard trap in a modal, saying "actually, that modal is scheduled for removal next sprint as part of a redesign."
contentSections.question: Which of these are legitimate reasons to actually revise the severity, versus reasons that shouldn't move it?

items.label: The barrier is genuinely going away soon, changing the real-world impact window
The engineering lead sounds annoyed
Downgrading would make the sprint easier to plan
A workaround genuinely exists that most affected users can reasonably find

explanation.a: A legitimate reason — severity should reflect real-world exposure, and a component's imminent removal is a real fact that changes that exposure.
explanation.b: Not a legitimate reason — tone or social discomfort isn't evidence about the barrier itself.
explanation.c: Not a legitimate reason — sprint planning convenience is an organisational pressure, not new evidence about user impact.
explanation.d: A legitimate reason, if the workaround is genuinely accessible and discoverable — this is real information about actual impact, which is exactly what severity should track.

contentSections.synthesis: The test in every case is the same: does the pushback introduce a genuine new fact about real-world impact, or is it pressure dressed up as a reason? Update the rating for the former; hold the line, calmly and with the original reasoning restated, against the latter.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it ever appropriate to say, in an interview, "I'd want to hear your reasoning before deciding whether to change it"?
contentSections.answer: Yes — this is often the strongest possible answer, because it demonstrates exactly the calibrated, evidence-based flexibility this lesson is teaching, rather than a scripted commitment to either concede or refuse in advance.
contentSections.hint: Consider whether an interviewer is looking for a fixed rule ("always hold firm" / "always defer") or a demonstrated process.

contentSections.body: Update a rating for a genuine new fact about impact. Hold it, calmly, against pressure that isn't evidence — and say which one you're responding to.

title: Interviewing while disabled, and what you owe nobody
description: What disability disclosure in a hiring process actually requires of a candidate, what accommodations are reasonable to request, and the firm line between relevant context and none of anyone's business.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate what a candidate owes an employer regarding disability disclosure during hiring

contentSections.title: What you're entitled to ask for

contentSections.body: A candidate assumes requesting an accommodation for an interview will be read as a weakness. In most well-run hiring processes, it's a completely routine administrative request — closer to asking for a different meeting time than to a confession.

contentSections.scenario: Reasonable accommodation requests for an interview process include: extra time for a timed exercise, written questions provided in advance, a remote or async alternative to a live panel, breaks between rounds, or a quieter/less visually busy interview environment.
contentSections.question: What do all of these requests have in common that makes them reasonable to ask for plainly, without extensive justification?

options.label: They're all free for the employer to provide
They change the format of the process without changing what's actually being evaluated
They're legally guaranteed in every country

feedback.free: Cost isn't really the common thread — some of these carry a small logistical cost, but that's true of many completely normal scheduling requests too.
feedback.format: Right. Extra time, written questions or a remote format change how the assessment is delivered, not what it measures — which is exactly why they're a normal, appropriate request rather than an advantage.
feedback.legal: Legal protections vary a great deal by country and employer size — the reasonableness of the request doesn't depend on which specific law applies where the candidate happens to be.

contentSections.concept: **An accommodation changes the format of an assessment, not its substance** — which is why requesting one is a routine administrative act, not a disclosure that needs defending.

contentSections.body: A request doesn't need to explain the underlying condition to be legitimate. "I'd like to request extra time for the technical exercise" is a complete, sufficient request on its own.
A reasonable accommodation changes the format of the process, not what's being measured — request it plainly, without a medical explanation attached.

contentSections.title: The line between context and none of their business

contentSections.body: Some disability context is genuinely useful to share, on your own terms — assistive technology fluency is a professional credential in this field, not a private fact. A diagnosis is a different category entirely.

contentSections.question: Order these disclosures from most useful to share voluntarily, to least appropriate for an employer to ask for.
steps: "I've used NVDA daily for six years, which is part of why I do this work well"
"I have a chronic condition that affects my energy levels day to day"
"Here's my specific diagnosis and how it was arrived at"
contentSections.explanation: Assistive technology fluency is professional context that directly supports a candidate's case — sharing it voluntarily is a strength, not a disclosure, and this track has treated it as exactly that since the foundations phase. A general statement about variable energy is sometimes useful in negotiating working patterns and is a candidate's choice to share, not an obligation. A specific diagnosis is the category furthest from anything an employer needs, and it's never appropriate for an interviewer to request it — declining that question cleanly, as covered in this lesson's practice, is a normal and complete answer.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does declining to answer a diagnosis question in an interview typically hurt a candidate's chances?
contentSections.answer: In a well-run process, no — a clean, confident decline ("that's not something I need to get into, but happy to talk through the accommodation itself") reads as boundary-setting, not evasiveness. If it visibly does hurt a candidate's chances, that's itself a strong warning sign about the employer, covered directly in the next lesson.
contentSections.hint: Consider what a reasonable interviewer would actually need the diagnosis for, versus what an unreasonable one might read into its absence.

contentSections.body: Share assistive-technology fluency freely — it's professional context. A diagnosis is never owed, and declining to share it is a complete, appropriate answer.

title: Assessing whether they'd be a decent employer
description: Reading the hiring process itself as evidence — how an employer handles an accommodation request, and whether they can point to a real, specific outcome, tells you more than anything on the careers page.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate hiring-process signals for whether an employer would resource accessibility work seriously

contentSections.title: The interview process previews the job

contentSections.body: How an organisation handles a candidate's accommodation request during hiring is a genuinely reliable preview of how it will handle accessibility findings after hiring — both are tests of whether inclusion holds up when it costs something small.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate requests extra time for a take-home exercise. Employer A grants it within an hour, no follow-up questions. Employer B grants it but sends two follow-up emails asking for more detail about "the nature of the need."
contentSections.question: What does Employer B's response most likely predict about how they'll handle an accessibility finding after hiring?

options.label: Nothing — hiring process and day-to-day work are unrelated
A tendency to require extra justification before acting, even once something is reasonably requested
That they don't care about accessibility at all

feedback.nothing: The two aren't unrelated — both are tests of whether a reasonable, low-cost request gets honoured without friction, which is a real organisational habit, not a one-off.
feedback.friction: Right. This is exactly the reverse-interview logic covered earlier in this track applied to a candidate's own experience — a pattern of requiring extra justification for something already reasonable is a genuine, transferable signal.
feedback.dontcare: Too strong a conclusion from one data point — it doesn't prove indifference, but it is a real, specific data point about process friction worth weighing seriously.

contentSections.concept: **The hiring process is itself an audit-able artefact.** How it handles a small, reasonable request under no real pressure previews how it will handle a real finding under real pressure later.

contentSections.body: How an employer handles a candidate's accommodation request is real evidence about how they'll handle a finding after hiring — weigh it accordingly.
The strongest way to get real information is still to ask a specific, hard-to-fake question — this module's whole approach applied one last time, from the other side of the table.

contentSections.question: Guess first: which is more revealing to ask an interviewer — "Is accessibility a priority here?" or "What happened the last time a finding conflicted with a deadline?"
contentSections.answer: The second, by a wide margin — it forces a specific, checkable example rather than an easy, costless affirmation. This is the same distinction this module has used from lesson one onward: specific and hard to fake beats general and easy to agree with.
contentSections.hint: Ask which question a company with no real track record could still answer smoothly.

contentSections.body: A short, high-signal set to have ready: "What happens to a finding after it's reported — who owns triaging it?" "Can you tell me about a real finding and what happened to it?" "What happens when a finding conflicts with a deadline?" None of these are confrontational to ask, and a reasonable interviewer will usually respect them — a defensive or evasive reaction to any of them is itself real information.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate asks the same "what happened to a real finding" question of a designer, an engineer and a hiring manager on the same team, across three separate rounds, and gets three noticeably different answers about how findings actually get resolved.
contentSections.question: What does that specific gap between the three answers most likely indicate?

options.label: One of the three is lying
Accessibility practice varies across the organisation and isn't consistently understood or owned end to end
Nothing — different roles are always expected to answer identically

feedback.lying: Not the likeliest explanation — three genuinely different, honest perspectives on the same process is common even in well-run organisations, and doesn't require dishonesty from anyone.
feedback.vary: Right. A real, consistent practice tends to produce roughly consistent answers across roles; a noticeable gap usually means the practice is patchy or unevenly owned, which is exactly the kind of thing worth knowing before accepting an offer.
feedback.nothing: Roles reasonably see different slices of the same process, but a genuinely inconsistent picture across all three is still a real, informative gap, not something to disregard.

contentSections.mechanism: Asking the same specific question of multiple people is a cheap way to test whether an organisation's accessibility practice is a real, shared system or a patchwork depending on who happens to care — and the size of the gap between answers is itself the signal.

contentSections.body: Ask for a specific, real example rather than a values statement — the answer, or the discomfort at being asked, tells you what you actually need to know.

title: Lab — Complete a Mock Take-Home Audit Under Real Constraints
description: Run a real, time-boxed take-home audit exercise on a live site of your choosing, then mark your own submission against the criteria a real employer would likely use.

learningObjectives.text: Apply staged, prioritised audit judgment under a real time constraint
Assess a completed submission against realistic hiring criteria

contentSections.body: The only way to know how you'll actually perform under a take-home's real time pressure is to run one for real, against a real site, with a clock — not to reason about it in the abstract.

contentSections.title: Your mock take-home audit
contentSections.brief: Pick a real, public page you don't already know well (a signup form, a checkout step, a booking flow) and give yourself a genuinely time-boxed window — 90 minutes is realistic — to audit it exactly as if it were a real take-home task. Then mark your own submission honestly against the criteria a real employer would likely use.
contentSections.deliverable: A completed take-home submission (prioritised findings with task impact, severity reasoning and at least one considered-and-rejected alternative fix) plus a written self-assessment scoring it against the rubric below.

stages.title: Scope and plan
stages.instructions: Pick the page and set a hard time limit. Decide up front, before starting the audit itself, roughly how you'll split the time between testing and writing — most candidates under-budget the writing time and it shows.
stages.checkpoint: You have a page, a time limit, and a rough time split written down before you start testing.

stages.title: Run the audit, staged
stages.instructions: Audit the page using the staged approach from the foundations phase — automated pass first, then manual and keyboard, narrowing scope explicitly if time runs short rather than rushing everything shallowly.
stages.checkpoint: You have real, specific findings with notes on task impact, not just a list of defects.

stages.title: Write the submission
stages.instructions: Write it exactly as you would submit it to a real employer: prioritised, task-impact-first findings, explicit severity reasoning, and an honest statement of what was and wasn't covered given the time.
stages.checkpoint: The submission is something you'd genuinely be willing to send.

stages.title: Self-assess against a marker's rubric
stages.instructions: Score your own submission against the rubric below as if you were the hiring manager, honestly — including naming where you'd have marked yourself down.
stages.checkpoint: You've named at least one real weakness in your own submission, not just its strengths.

rubric.criterion: Findings are prioritised by task impact, not scan output order
rubric.meets: The first finding presented is genuinely the most severe, with reasoning, not just the first one noticed.

rubric.criterion: Severity reasoning is explicit
rubric.meets: Each finding states why it earned its rating, not just a label.

rubric.criterion: Scope is honestly stated if time ran short
rubric.meets: A reader can tell exactly what was and wasn't covered, without guessing.

rubric.criterion: At least one finding shows real judgment beyond an obvious automated result
rubric.meets: Something in the submission required manual testing or reasoning a scanner couldn't have produced alone.

contentSections.body: Running this once, honestly, under a real clock, tells you more about your interview readiness than any amount of reading about it would.

title: Auditing in stages that fit a real energy budget
description: Extending the staged-audit habit from the foundations phase into a repeatable weekly practice — buffer built in from the start, not improvised after a bad day arrives.

learningObjectives.text: Design an engagement schedule that treats variable capacity as a planning input, not an exception

contentSections.title: Buffer as a default, not a rescue

contentSections.body: A three-week audit is scoped at exactly three weeks of full-capacity work. It has no room in it for a bad week at all — which means the plan was never really a plan for how the work would actually go, only for how it would go if nothing went wrong.

contentSections.scenario: Two ways of scoping the same three-week audit. **A.** Three weeks of work, scheduled across three weeks. **B.** Three weeks of work, scheduled across four weeks, with the fourth held as unscheduled buffer from the start.
contentSections.question: Which plan actually survives a genuinely bad week without a renegotiation conversation?

options.label: A
B

feedback.a: This plan looks identical to B until the first bad week, at which point it requires exactly the renegotiation conversation from the foundations phase — every time, because there was never any slack to absorb it.
feedback.b: Right. A held buffer week means a bad week costs a week, not a client conversation and a scope cut — the plan already accounted for it.

contentSections.concept: **A buffer isn't a rescue plan improvised after a bad day — it's a default built into the schedule before the engagement starts**, the same way the foundations phase's staged audit made every boundary a defensible stopping point.

contentSections.body: This doesn't mean quoting every engagement at 25% longer automatically — a genuinely predictable, low-complexity audit may not need it. It means the buffer decision is made deliberately, up front, as part of scoping, rather than discovered under pressure mid-engagement.
Decide the buffer at scoping time, not mid-engagement — a held week costs nothing until it's needed, and everything if it isn't there.

The foundations phase staged the audit methodology — automated, then keyboard, then screen reader. A sustainable practice stages the whole engagement the same way, including the parts that aren't testing at all.

contentSections.question: Put these engagement activities in the order that puts the least essential, hardest-to-interrupt work last, so a bad week costs the least.
steps: Screen reader and detailed manual testing
contentSections.explanation: This mirrors the foundations-phase staging logic exactly, applied to the whole engagement: scoping is essential and low-effort to redo if delayed; automated and keyboard testing is high-value and relatively low-cognitive-load; screen reader work demands more sustained focus; and report writing, while not physically demanding, requires the clearest thinking of the whole engagement and is worth protecting for a better day rather than rushing on a bad one.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does staging by activity type, rather than by client deliverable, cost more calendar time overall?
contentSections.answer: Not usually — the total work is the same either way. What changes is where the natural stopping points fall, so an interruption costs a stage, not a scramble to finish whatever happened to be in progress.
contentSections.hint: Compare the total hours of work in each approach, not just how it's sequenced.

contentSections.body: Stage the whole engagement, not just the testing — protect the highest-focus work (report writing) for the days it's actually available.

title: The emotional cost of finding the same barrier repeatedly
description: What to do with the real fatigue of writing the same preventable finding for the twentieth time, without either burning out or going numb to it.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate strategies for managing the recurring emotional cost of repetitive findings

contentSections.title: The specific fatigue this work produces

contentSections.body: It's not the difficulty of finding a missing accessible name that wears a reviewer down after the fiftieth time. It's writing the same explanation of why it matters, to a team that's never heard it before, again.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer with three years of experience describes feeling numb rather than frustrated when they find the same common barrier now, and worries this means they've stopped caring.
contentSections.question: What's a more accurate read of what's actually happened?

options.label: They genuinely no longer care about the impact of the barrier
The explanatory labour has become routine and depleting in a specific, addressable way — separate from whether the underlying impact still matters to them
This means they should leave the field

feedback.nocare: Numbness toward the *repetition* of explaining something is a different thing from no longer caring about the *impact* — most reviewers who feel this way still care intensely when they see the actual barrier block a real task; it's the twentieth explanation of the same mechanism that's worn thin.
feedback.routine: Right. This is exactly the gap the template-library practice from lesson one addresses — separating the part that's become routine (re-explaining a familiar mechanism) from the part that still requires genuine care (this specific instance, this specific client).
feedback.leave: Too large a conclusion from this specific, addressable symptom — plenty of experienced reviewers feel this and stay, once the routine part is handled differently.

contentSections.mechanism: The fatigue often isn't about the barrier itself losing meaning — it's the unpaid emotional labour of re-explaining a familiar mechanism from scratch every time, which a template and a clearer boundary around what deserves fresh energy can genuinely relieve.

contentSections.body: Numbness toward repeating an explanation isn't the same as no longer caring about the barrier — treat the two differently.

contentSections.title: When it's a signal worth acting on

contentSections.body: Some recurring frustration is just the ordinary texture of this work. Some of it is a real signal. Telling the two apart matters, because acting on the wrong one either burns a reviewer out unnecessarily or misses a genuine warning sign.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer notices several things about how they've felt over the last two months.
contentSections.question: Which of these are closer to a genuine burnout signal worth acting on, versus ordinary recurring frustration?

items.label: Frustration at finding the same missing-alt-text pattern on a new client's site
Dread before starting every new engagement, not just occasional ones
Catching themselves pasting a template finding without checking whether it actually fits this instance
Feeling tired at the end of a screen reader testing day

explanation.a: Ordinary — a specific, familiar, preventable pattern reasonably produces mild frustration each time; it doesn't indicate a bigger problem on its own.
explanation.b: A real signal — dread that's generalised across all engagements, rather than tied to a specific difficult client or barrier, points at something beyond ordinary recurring frustration.
explanation.c: A real signal — this is the exact quality failure a template is supposed to prevent; catching it happening is worth treating as a warning, not just a one-off slip.
explanation.d: Ordinary — screen reader testing is genuinely demanding, focused work; being tired afterward is a normal cost of the activity, not a burnout indicator on its own.

contentSections.synthesis: The pattern separating a real signal from ordinary texture: generalised dread (not tied to a specific cause) and templates degrading into unchecked copy-paste are both worth acting on directly — with a schedule change, a break, or reconsidering the mix of audit and other work covered in the next lessons. Ordinary task fatigue and familiar-pattern frustration are the normal cost of doing real work, not a problem to solve away.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it reasonable to pair audit work with occasional advocacy or systemic work specifically to relieve recurring-barrier fatigue?
contentSections.answer: Yes, for many reviewers — seeing the same preventable barrier repeatedly is itself an argument for spending some energy on the earlier phase's advocacy work, which addresses causes rather than instances, and can genuinely offset the fatigue of purely repeated individual findings.
contentSections.hint: Consider what kind of work targets the root pattern rather than the next instance of it.

contentSections.body: Generalised dread and a degrading template are real signals worth acting on. Familiar-pattern frustration and task fatigue are the normal cost of the work.

title: Being the only disabled person in the room
description: Holding a professional boundary when you're the sole disabled voice in a meeting — what you're there to offer, what you're not obligated to carry, and where to find the peer perspective a single reviewer can't provide alone.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate the boundary between offering professional and lived-experience authority and being expected to represent all disabled people

contentSections.title: What you're actually there to offer

contentSections.body: A product manager, mid-meeting, turns to the one visibly disabled person in the room and asks, "So what do disabled people actually think of this?" — a question with an answer nobody could actually give, asked as though the reviewer could give it.

contentSections.scenario: Three possible responses to that exact question in the meeting. **A.** Attempt a confident answer covering disabled people broadly. **B.** Say nothing, uncomfortable with the framing but unsure how to redirect it. **C.** "I can tell you what I'm seeing in this specific flow and my own experience with it — for a fuller picture across different disabilities, that's what user testing with a range of participants would give you."
contentSections.question: Which response protects both the reviewer's credibility and the actual quality of the answer the room gets?

options.label: A
B
C

feedback.a: This overclaims authority no single person has, and risks the room mistaking one person's answer for a comprehensive one — which can actually reduce the pressure to do real user testing later.
feedback.b: Understandable in the moment, but it leaves the framing unchallenged and misses a chance to redirect the room toward what would actually answer the question.
feedback.c: Right. This offers real, specific value — professional judgment plus genuine lived experience — while naming clearly what would actually be needed for the broader question, which is more useful to the room than either overclaiming or staying silent.

contentSections.concept: **A reviewer's presence in the room is evidence about their own perspective, not a substitute for testing with a range of real users.** Naming that distinction plainly is professional, not defensive.

contentSections.body: This isn't a one-time script — it's a boundary worth having ready before the moment arrives, because it arrives more often than most reviewers expect, and improvising it under mild social pressure in the room is harder than saying it once, clearly, in advance.
Offer your own professional and lived-experience authority plainly. Redirect requests to represent everyone toward what would actually answer that — real testing with real range.

contentSections.title: Where the actual peer perspective comes from

contentSections.body: If the room can't give a reviewer the peer context a single seat never can, the search for it has to happen somewhere else — deliberately, not as an afterthought.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a realistic plan for getting peer perspective outside the client room.

options: Assume your own experience generalises closely enough
Disability-led professional communities and forums outside any single client relationship
Wait for a client to arrange it
fields.correctValue: Disability-led professional communities and forums outside any single client relationship
fields.feedback: A community of peers, independent of any one client engagement, is where the range a single reviewer's seat can't provide actually lives.

options: Only after a client explicitly asks for broader perspective
As an ongoing practice, independent of any specific engagement
Never — it's not a professional responsibility
fields.correctValue: As an ongoing practice, independent of any specific engagement
fields.feedback: Built as an ongoing practice, this is available the moment a room asks the impossible question — rather than something scrambled together under pressure.

options: Cite it as if it were your own direct experience
Recommend it explicitly as a resource — a workshop, a testing panel, a community — rather than trying to individually represent it
Keep it entirely separate from client work
fields.correctValue: Recommend it explicitly as a resource — a workshop, a testing panel, a community — rather than trying to individually represent it
fields.feedback: Naming a real resource (a testing panel, a disability-led consultancy for a fuller review) is more useful and more honest than trying to personally carry weight it was never one person's job to carry.

contentSections.synthesis: None of this replaces what a single reviewer offers — it supplements it, and makes the boundary from earlier in this lesson easier to hold in the moment, because there's a real, specific resource to point toward instead of just a polite decline.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does naming this boundary explicitly in a client meeting typically damage a reviewer's professional standing?
contentSections.answer: Generally no — in a well-run engagement, it reads as exactly what it is: professional clarity about the limits of any one person's authority, which most serious clients respect once it's said plainly and paired with a real next step.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to how a doctor might decline to speak for a whole patient population beyond their own clinical judgment.

contentSections.body: Build the peer-context relationships before you need them in the room — then you have something real to point to, not just a boundary to defend alone.

title: Boundaries around unpaid education
description: Telling apart the occasional, deliberately chosen unpaid opportunity from unpaid work becoming the default response to every ask — and how to decline the latter without burning the relationship.

learningObjectives.text: Construct a boundary policy for unpaid education requests that protects sustainability without foreclosing genuine relationship-building

contentSections.title: The ask that sounds like a favour and isn't

contentSections.body: "Just a quick 30-minute chat with the team, no pressure" is a real request for a real deliverable — a training session — described in language that makes declining feel disproportionate.

contentSections.code:
Email from a former client:

"Hey! Would love to pick your brain for 30 min with the whole eng team on accessibility basics sometime. No pressure, totally informal, would be great exposure for you with our team!"
contentSections.question: What makes this request easy to say yes to reflexively, and why is that worth resisting?

options.label: It's framed as small and informal, when it's actually a scoped training session for a whole team
The client is being manipulative on purpose
"Exposure" always means the request should be declined outright

feedback.framing: Right. "Quick," "informal" and "no pressure" describe the tone, not the actual scope — a real session with an entire engineering team is genuine, valuable consulting work regardless of how casually it's framed.
feedback.manip: Most requests like this aren't made in bad faith — the client likely doesn't see it as asking for unpaid labour at all, which is exactly why the framing matters more than intent here.
feedback.always: Too absolute — this lesson isn't arguing every unpaid request should be declined outright, just that the reflexive yes deserves a second look.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The fix isn't necessarily refusal — it's re-scoping the request accurately: "Happy to do that — I'd frame it as a proper session so I can actually prepare well for your team, here's what that would look like," which reframes the same request as the real deliverable it is, on paid terms.

contentSections.body: Casual framing doesn't change the actual scope of a request — re-scope it accurately before deciding whether it's worth doing unpaid.

contentSections.title: When unpaid is a genuine, deliberate choice

contentSections.body: A default of "no unpaid work" is easier to hold than a case-by-case judgment call every time — but it's also not quite what this lesson is arguing for.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer accepts an unpaid slot speaking at a small, disability-led community conference, and separately declines a former client's unpaid team training request the same month.
contentSections.question: What actually distinguishes the accepted request from the declined one?

options.label: One is bigger than the other
The accepted one was chosen deliberately for its own value to the reviewer, not as a default reflex to an ask framed as small
Community events should always be free and client requests never should be

feedback.size: Size isn't the actual variable — a small community talk and a 30-minute team session are similar in scope; what differs is why each one was said yes or no to.
feedback.deliberate: Right. The conference talk was a considered choice made for reasons that matter to the reviewer — visibility in a community they value. The team training request was close to a reflexive yes to a familiar, casually-framed ask. Same category of request, different process behind the answer.
feedback.rule: Too rigid a rule for what this lesson is actually teaching — the distinction is about intentionality, not a blanket category split between community and corporate asks.

contentSections.mechanism: The sustainable version of this boundary isn't a hard no to every unpaid request — it's converting every request into a deliberate choice, rather than letting the ones with the softest framing default to yes.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it reasonable to have a standard, prepared response for declining unpaid team-training requests, used consistently?
contentSections.answer: Yes — a prepared, consistent response (like the re-scoping move from earlier in this lesson) removes the energy cost of deciding fresh each time and makes it much easier to hold the boundary under the mild social pressure of a friendly-sounding ask.
contentSections.hint: Compare this to how a template finding saves energy on boilerplate while a fresh judgment is still applied to what matters.

contentSections.body: Convert every unpaid request into a deliberate choice — not a reflex to friendly framing, and not a blanket refusal either.

title: Choosing clients who will actually fix things
description: Screening a prospective client, before bidding, for whether they intend to act on findings or are commissioning an audit mainly to file away.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate prospective-client signals for genuine remediation intent before committing to an engagement

contentSections.title: The engagement that was never going to change anything

contentSections.body: A reviewer spends three weeks on a thorough, well-written audit. Eight months later, nothing on the site has changed, and a follow-up email gets no reply. The findings weren't wrong. They were never going to be acted on, and there were signals of that before the engagement even started.

contentSections.scenario: An RFP for an accessibility audit states: "Deliverable: a report we can reference for our annual accessibility statement." It doesn't mention engineering involvement, a remediation budget, or a timeline anywhere in the document.
contentSections.question: What does the RFP's own language, read carefully, suggest about the likely purpose of this engagement?

options.label: Nothing meaningful — most RFPs are written this way regardless of intent
The framing centres the report as the deliverable itself, with no mention of what happens to the findings afterward — a real, checkable warning sign
It guarantees the client won't fix anything

feedback.nothing: The specific absence here is worth noticing — a genuinely remediation-focused RFP usually says something, even briefly, about what happens after the report lands.
feedback.warning: Right. This mirrors the earlier lesson's evidence-sorting exercise directly: a deliverable framed entirely around the report itself, with remediation nowhere in the document, is a real, specific, checkable signal worth probing before bidding.
feedback.guarantee: Too strong — it's a signal to investigate further, via direct questions, not a certainty on its own.

contentSections.concept: **Read what an RFP or brief centres as the deliverable.** A report framed as the end product, with no mention of what happens next, is worth a direct follow-up question before committing real weeks to it.

contentSections.body: An RFP that frames the report itself as the deliverable, with remediation unmentioned, is worth a direct question before bidding — not a reason to assume the worst outright.

contentSections.title: Walking away, and what it costs either way

contentSections.body: Declining a checkbox-only engagement costs real, immediate income. Taking it costs weeks of real effort on findings that were statistically unlikely to matter — and every practice built across this whole module exists partly to make that second cost visible enough to weigh properly.

contentSections.scenario: Among audit engagements where the RFP or kickoff conversation shows none of the remediation-intent signals from this lesson (no engineering involvement, no budget, no timeline discussed).
contentSections.question: Roughly what share, anecdotally reported by experienced reviewers, result in genuinely no visible remediation a year later?
contentSections.explanation: The precise figure varies by who's reporting it, but the consistent pattern experienced reviewers describe is that the absence of remediation-intent signals at the start predicts the absence of remediation at the end, far more often than not. This is exactly why screening for it before bidding — not just noticing it with regret afterward — is the actual skill this lesson is teaching.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it ever worth taking a likely checkbox-only engagement anyway?
contentSections.answer: Sometimes, deliberately — for income during a lean period, or because even an unread report can occasionally be cited by an advocate later. The key word is deliberately: taking it as an informed trade-off is different from taking it because the signals were never checked.
contentSections.hint: Consider whether this lesson is arguing for an absolute rule or for making the choice with full information.

contentSections.body: Screen for remediation intent before bidding, not after delivering — the signals are usually visible early, and taking a checkbox-only engagement anyway is a fine choice as long as it's an informed one.

Produce a working agreement a real client could read and act on

title: WCAG versions and what actually changed
description: What genuinely changed between WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2 — additive, not replacements — and what's actually different about the 3.0 work in progress.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what changed between WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2, and how those versions relate to each other

contentSections.body: A reviewer new to the field assumes WCAG 2.2 replaces 2.0 the way a new phone model replaces an old one — newer, better, the old one obsolete. That's not how these versions relate to each other, and the difference matters the first time a contract names a specific one.

contentSections.scenario: WCAG 2.0 (2008) is the original, widely-cited baseline. WCAG 2.1 (2018) kept every 2.0 success criterion and added new ones — mainly covering mobile accessibility, low vision, and cognitive/learning disabilities. WCAG 2.2 (2023) kept everything from 2.0 and 2.1 and added further criteria — including focus appearance, dragging alternatives, minimum target size, accessible authentication, and consistent help placement.
contentSections.question: What does auditing to "WCAG 2.0 AA" leave uncovered that auditing to "WCAG 2.2 AA" would include?

options.label: Nothing — 2.0 already covers everything the later versions do
All of the mobile, low-vision, cognitive and later criteria added in 2.1 and 2.2
Only cosmetic wording differences

feedback.nothing: Backwards — 2.0 is the smaller set. Each later version adds criteria on top of it rather than the reverse.
feedback.later: Right. A 2.0-only audit genuinely doesn't test against the mobile, low-vision, cognitive, target-size or authentication-related criteria added afterward — this isn't a wording nuance, it's a real scope difference.
feedback.cosmetic: The differences are substantive new success criteria, not just rewording of the existing ones.

contentSections.concept: **Every WCAG version since 2.0 is additive.** 2.1 kept all of 2.0 and added to it; 2.2 kept all of 2.1 (and therefore 2.0) and added further to that. Naming the specific version in scope is a real, checkable claim about what was and wasn't tested — not a formality.

contentSections.body: Practically, this means a legacy contract naming "2.0 AA" isn't wrong or outdated to honour as written — it's a real, narrower scope, worth naming plainly and worth raising with the client as a conversation about updating the target, rather than silently testing to a broader version and calling it the same thing.
2.1 and 2.2 add to 2.0 rather than replacing it — naming the exact version in scope is a real, checkable claim, not a formality.

contentSections.title: What's coming, and what isn't yet

contentSections.body: WCAG 3.0 gets mentioned often enough in industry conversation that it's worth knowing what it actually is — and, just as importantly, what it isn't yet.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is WCAG 3.0 close to replacing 2.x in real client contracts right now?
contentSections.answer: No — it remains in active development, with a genuinely different, more graded scoring approach than 2.x's binary pass/fail, but it's years from being finalised or broadly adopted. Treating it as imminent would misinform a client planning today's work.
contentSections.hint: Weigh how long a W3C spec of this scope typically takes to move from draft to widely-adopted standard.

contentSections.body: The one concrete thing worth knowing now: 3.0 is aiming for a different structure than a single pass/fail per criterion — something closer to graded, weighted scoring across a broader set of outcomes. That's a real, notable shift in direction, and it's also not something to bring into a live engagement's scope discussion as though it were close to ready.

contentSections.scenario: A candidate in an interview says, confidently, "WCAG 3.0 is basically finalised and most of the industry has already moved to it."
contentSections.question: What does this claim most likely reveal?

options.label: Accurate, current knowledge of the spec's status
A misunderstanding of how far 3.0 actually is from adoption
Nothing meaningful either way

feedback.accurate: This doesn't match the real state of 3.0's development — it remains years from being finalised or broadly adopted in contracts.
feedback.misunderstanding: Right. This is exactly the overclaim this lesson is built to prevent — knowing 3.0 exists and knowing it's imminent are two very different claims, and only the first is currently accurate.
feedback.nothing: It's meaningful — overstating a spec's readiness to a client or interviewer is a real, checkable knowledge gap, not a neutral detail.

contentSections.mechanism: Staying current means being accurate about a change's actual status, not just aware that it exists — an inflated claim about 3.0's readiness is arguably worse than not knowing about it at all, since it could shape a client's real planning decisions.

contentSections.body: Know that 3.0 is coming and roughly how it will differ in structure — and be equally clear that it isn't close to displacing 2.x in real contracts yet.

title: Assistive tech updates that change your findings
description: Why a finding verified with one screen reader and browser pairing doesn't automatically generalise, and what actually changes when assistive technology updates.

learningObjectives.text: Analyse how assistive technology and browser updates can change the accuracy of an existing finding

contentSections.body: A finding verified as "passes" with NVDA and Firefox gets copied into a report as a flat statement of fact. Six weeks later, the same client's own QA team files a bug: the identical pattern fails with JAWS and Chrome.

contentSections.scenario: The same custom dropdown component announces its selected value correctly in NVDA with Firefox, but announces nothing at all in JAWS with Chrome.
contentSections.question: What's the most likely explanation?

options.label: The JAWS user is doing something wrong
Different screen reader and browser combinations implement the accessibility tree and ARIA mapping slightly differently, and this pattern happens to expose that difference
This is impossible — accessible markup behaves identically everywhere

feedback.user: There's no reason to assume user error here — a genuine markup-to-announcement gap in one specific pairing is a common, well-documented pattern.
feedback.combo: Right. Screen reader and browser pairs don't implement ARIA and the accessibility tree identically, and a pattern that works fine in one pairing can genuinely fail in another — this is exactly why testing across the relevant pairings, not just one, matters.
feedback.impossible: Not impossible at all — this kind of pairing-specific divergence is one of the most common reasons a finding needs to state which environment it was actually verified in.

contentSections.mechanism: A finding is only as reliable as the environment it was tested in. Reporting a result as universal when it was verified in one pairing overstates what was actually checked.

contentSections.body: A finding verified in one screen reader/browser pairing doesn't automatically hold in another — state which pairing was tested, or test the ones that actually matter for the client's users.

contentSections.title: What genuinely changes with an update

contentSections.body: Not every AT release note matters equally. Some updates fix bugs a reviewer never relied on; others change exactly the behaviour a past finding assumed was stable.

contentSections.scenario: A major screen reader's release notes for its latest version.
contentSections.question: Which of these release-note items would most plausibly require retesting an existing finding?

items.label: "Fixed: live regions with aria-live='polite' now correctly queue multiple rapid updates"
"Updated: installer now supports an additional language pack"
"Changed: default verbosity for landmark announcements adjusted"
"Improved: startup time reduced by 200ms"

explanation.a: Directly relevant — a change to how live regions queue updates could change whether a past finding about a live-region pattern still holds.
explanation.b: Unrelated to audit findings — a language pack addition doesn't touch how existing markup is announced.
explanation.c: Directly relevant — a changed default verbosity for landmarks could change what a past finding about landmark navigation actually observed.
explanation.d: Unrelated — a performance improvement doesn't change announcement behaviour.

contentSections.synthesis: Scanning release notes for behavioural changes — not every line item — is what makes this sustainable. The two irrelevant items here cost nothing to skip; the two relevant ones are exactly what a quarterly retest, covered later in this module, should sample against.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it worth maintaining a short, fixed list of the AT/browser pairings you actually verify against, rather than trying to track every possible combination?
contentSections.answer: Yes — a short, deliberately chosen list (matched to the client base you actually serve) is what makes staying current sustainable, echoing the earlier module's point about a fixed weekly energy budget applied to tooling breadth instead of time.
contentSections.hint: Weigh the number of possible AT/browser/OS combinations against what's realistic to verify every quarter.

contentSections.body: Scan release notes for behavioural changes specifically, and keep a short, deliberately chosen list of pairings you actually verify against — not an attempt to track everything.

title: Platform and browser changes worth watching
description: How native element behaviour, browser accessibility-tree implementations and OS-level changes can quietly change whether an old finding or fix is still accurate.

learningObjectives.text: Analyse how platform and browser changes affect the currency of existing findings

contentSections.title: When the platform starts doing the work for you

contentSections.body: A finding written two years ago recommends a specific ARIA pattern to build an accessible modal from scratch. The browser has since shipped a native `<dialog>` element with built-in focus-trapping behaviour. The old recommendation isn't wrong, exactly — it's no longer the best available answer.

contentSections.scenario: Two facts: **(1)** The native `<dialog>` element, once niche, now ships with built-in focus management and top-layer rendering in modern browsers. **(2)** A reviewer has an existing finding recommending a custom `role="dialog"` implementation with a manually coded focus trap, written before this native support matured.
contentSections.question: What's the right next step for that existing finding?

options.label: Leave it exactly as written — it was correct when written, so it stays correct
Re-evaluate whether the native element is now the better recommendation, given the platform has changed since the finding was written
Assume every custom modal implementation in existence is now automatically wrong

feedback.leave: A finding's currency is tied to the platform it was written against — when the platform genuinely changes, the finding is worth a fresh look, not an assumption of permanent correctness.
feedback.reeval: Right. This is exactly the retesting judgment this module is building — a platform-level change can make an old recommendation outdated without making it was ever wrong at the time.
feedback.assume: Too broad a conclusion — plenty of custom modal implementations remain necessary or well-built; the point is to check specifically, not condemn a whole category.

contentSections.concept: **A platform-level change — a new native element, a browser exposing something differently to the accessibility tree — can move the correct recommendation without the original finding having been wrong.** This is a different kind of drift than an AT update, and it's worth watching separately.

contentSections.body: Other platform-level changes worth tracking the same way: new HTML elements or attributes gaining semantic meaning (like the `popover` attribute), a browser changing how it exposes computed accessible names, or a mobile OS updating its accessibility API in a way that changes what a native app framework provides for free.
A native platform change can move the best recommendation without the original finding having been wrong when it was written — check specifically rather than assuming permanence in either direction.
The list of things that could theoretically change is unbounded. A sustainable practice doesn't track everything — it tracks the handful of sources likely to actually matter.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a realistic, bounded set of platform sources worth actually watching.

options: Every individual browser changelog entry, unfiltered
Release notes filtered specifically for accessibility-tree, ARIA and focus-related changes
Nothing — browser changes rarely matter
fields.correctValue: Release notes filtered specifically for accessibility-tree, ARIA and focus-related changes
fields.feedback: Filtering for the specific category of change that affects findings, rather than reading every changelog entry, is what keeps this sustainable.

options: The full WHATWG HTML living standard, read in full each quarter
A curated summary of newly-semantic elements and attributes (like the WAI or a trusted community digest)
Nothing — new elements rarely matter for accessibility
fields.correctValue: A curated summary of newly-semantic elements and attributes (like the WAI or a trusted community digest)
fields.feedback: A curated digest does the filtering work for you — the full living standard is not a sustainable quarterly read for this specific purpose.

options: Full OS release notes, unfiltered
Accessibility-specific release notes or a trusted community summary for the platforms your clients' users actually use
Skip mobile entirely
fields.correctValue: Accessibility-specific release notes or a trusted community summary for the platforms your clients' users actually use
fields.feedback: Scoped to the platforms actually relevant to your work, this stays inside a sustainable quarterly budget rather than becoming an unbounded task.

contentSections.synthesis: Every choice here follows the same principle: filtered, curated, and scoped to what's actually relevant to your work — not an attempt to read everything that changes, which is exactly the pattern the next lesson's community list and the final lesson's quarterly routine both build on.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it worth re-testing every past finding whenever a platform change is spotted?
contentSections.answer: No — sample a representative subset likely to be affected, the same way an AT update is handled. Re-testing everything on every change isn't sustainable and isn't necessary; most findings are unaffected by any given change.
contentSections.hint: Consider how many findings a typical reviewer has accumulated over a career, and what re-testing all of them on every platform update would actually cost.

contentSections.body: Filter platform sources down to accessibility-tree, semantic and focus-relevant changes specifically, scoped to what your clients actually use — and sample, don't re-test everything.

title: Communities worth being in
description: Which communities and resources actually keep a reviewer current, what each is best for, and why low-energy lurking counts as real participation.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate which communities and resources serve which specific currency need

contentSections.body: "Just follow the accessibility community" isn't actionable advice — the community isn't one thing, and a reviewer who tries to follow all of it equally ends up following none of it well.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer wants to know the emerging consensus on how to correctly build a combobox pattern.
contentSections.question: Which resource is best matched to that specific question?

options.label: The W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide's issue tracker and published patterns
A general disability-led community Discord
A conference's published talk recordings from two years ago

feedback.aria: Right. The APG is specifically where pattern-level consensus for complex widgets is actively debated and published — the closest thing this field has to an authoritative, current reference for exactly this question.
feedback.discord: A general community is valuable for other things — lived-experience perspective, real-world discussion — but it's not the most direct source for a specific technical pattern consensus question.
feedback.conf: Conference talks are useful for depth, but a two-year-old recording risks being outdated on a fast-moving pattern question specifically.

contentSections.concept: **Match the source to the specific kind of currency it's actually good at providing.** Pattern consensus, real-world usage data, lived-experience perspective and deep case-study material are four different needs, best served by four different kinds of source.

contentSections.body: Different sources serve different currency needs — match the question to the source built to answer it, rather than treating "the community" as one undifferentiated feed.
A reviewer feels they're not "really" part of the accessibility community because they read far more than they post. That's a real, sustainable form of participation, not a lesser one.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer with limited energy this month reads community discussion threads regularly but hasn't posted or commented in weeks.
contentSections.question: What's the accurate way to think about this pattern of engagement?

options.label: It provides no real value until they start posting actively
Reading alone still surfaces real usage patterns and current discussion, at a lower energy cost than active posting — a genuinely sustainable form of staying current
They should force themselves to post more to get real value

feedback.novalue: Too strict — the value of a community as a currency source doesn't require active posting; reading is doing the actual job of staying current.
feedback.value: Right. This mirrors the earlier module's point about a documentation fix counting as a full, legitimate open-source contribution on a lower-energy day — reading-only community engagement is the equivalent for staying current.
feedback.force: Unnecessary, and potentially counterproductive — forcing active participation to feel legitimate adds an energy cost this lesson is specifically arguing isn't required.

contentSections.mechanism: The goal of community engagement in this context is staying current, not building a public profile — and reading alone accomplishes the former completely, at whatever energy level a given week allows.

contentSections.question: Guess first: does it matter which specific platform (Slack, Discord, a mailing list, a forum) a community lives on?
contentSections.answer: Less than the content and moderation quality — a well-moderated, active community on any platform beats a quiet one on a trendier platform. Pick based on where the specific discussion you need is actually happening.
contentSections.hint: Consider whether the platform itself, or what's discussed on it, is the thing actually providing currency.

contentSections.body: Reading without posting is real, sustainable participation — pick communities for what they're actually good at, and let energy that week determine how actively you engage.

title: A quarterly refresh routine
description: A repeatable, time-boxed routine that turns everything else in this module — spec versions, AT updates, platform changes, community sources — into a fixed quarterly habit rather than an unbounded, anxiety-inducing task.

learningObjectives.text: Design a repeatable, time-boxed currency review routine

contentSections.title: Turning "stay current" into a routine with an edge

contentSections.body: "Stay current with everything in the field" is an unbounded task with no natural stopping point — which is exactly the kind of task that either gets skipped entirely or quietly consumes far more time than it should. A routine with a fixed shape and a fixed time budget fixes both problems at once.

contentSections.question: Put these four steps of a quarterly review in the order that makes the routine actually sustainable, cheapest and most informative first.
steps: Scan release notes and spec updates since the last review, filtered for behavioural changes
Choose a small, representative sample of past findings or common patterns likely to be affected
Retest that sample directly against the current environment
Write up what changed and exactly which past findings, if any, it revises
contentSections.explanation: This is the same order built across this module's earlier lessons, brought together into one routine: scan first because it's cheap and tells you where to focus; sample deliberately rather than retesting everything; retest for real evidence rather than assumption; and document the outcome so the review produces a usable artefact, not just private study.

contentSections.body: Scan, sample, retest, document — in that order, every quarter, on a fixed time budget.
A currency routine that takes three days every quarter won't survive contact with a real practice. One sized to a half-day will.

contentSections.scenario: A reviewer runs this four-step routine for the first time, scoped to a handful of sources and a small retest sample as described in this lesson.
contentSections.question: Roughly how long does a well-scoped version of this routine take, in hours?
contentSections.explanation: The specific number will vary by how many sources and how large a retest sample a reviewer chooses, but a well-scoped version — a handful of filtered sources, a small representative sample, not an attempt at exhaustive coverage — comfortably fits inside half a working day. If a first attempt takes much longer than that, the fix is usually narrowing the source list or the sample size next time, not accepting that staying current requires a much larger time budget.

contentSections.question: Guess first: is it worth running this routine more often than quarterly, to catch changes faster?
contentSections.answer: Usually not — most of what this routine tracks (spec versions, major AT releases, platform changes) doesn't move fast enough to need more frequent review, and a shorter interval mostly just adds overhead without much additional signal. Quarterly is a reasonable default; a genuinely fast-moving period (a major AT release, a new WCAG version) is worth an off-cycle check, not a permanently shorter interval.
contentSections.hint: Weigh how often the actual underlying sources — spec versions, major releases — genuinely change against the fixed cost of running the routine.

contentSections.body: Size the routine to fit inside half a day — if it doesn't, narrow the source list or the sample before assuming staying current requires more time than that.

title: Lab — Run One Quarterly Currency Review
description: Run the module's four-step routine for real, against real sources and a real sample of past findings or common patterns, and produce the write-up naming what changed and what it revises.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's currency-review routine to a real set of sources and findings
Produce a review document naming exactly what changed and which findings it revises

contentSections.body: The routine only proves itself sustainable by actually being run once, against real material, inside the time budget this module has been building toward — not by being reasoned about in the abstract.

contentSections.title: Your quarterly currency review
contentSections.brief: Run a real currency review: scan for genuine changes since you last paid attention (or since this track began, if this is your first), pick a small sample of past findings or common patterns to retest, retest them, and write up exactly what changed and which findings it revises.
contentSections.deliverable: A short review document listing the sources checked, what changed, the sample retested, and — explicitly — which past findings or patterns are revised, confirmed unaffected, or need further checking.

stages.title: Scan for changes
stages.instructions: Check for updates against the filtered categories from this module: WCAG/spec changes, a couple of AT release notes, one or two platform/browser changes, and a skim of one community source. Note only the items that plausibly affect real findings, not everything you see.
stages.checkpoint: You have a short, specific list of changes worth investigating further — not an exhaustive log of everything read.

stages.title: Pick a sample and retest
stages.instructions: Choose two or three past findings or common patterns (from your own portfolio, practice audits, or well-known patterns from this track) that the scan suggests might be affected. Retest them directly in the current environment.
stages.checkpoint: You have real retest results for each item in the sample, not just a guess about what probably changed.

stages.title: Write the review
stages.instructions: Write the document exactly as the deliverable describes: sources checked, what changed, what was retested, and the explicit verdict for each — revised, confirmed unaffected, or needs further checking.
stages.checkpoint: A reader could tell exactly what's still current and what isn't, without guessing.

rubric.criterion: Sources checked are named specifically
rubric.meets: Lists the actual spec, AT, platform and community sources checked, not a vague "stayed current this quarter."

rubric.criterion: The sample is real and relevant
rubric.meets: Retested items are genuinely plausible candidates for having changed, based on the scan, not chosen at random.

rubric.criterion: Retest results are concrete
rubric.meets: States what was actually observed on retest, not just a restated assumption.

rubric.criterion: The verdict is explicit for each item
rubric.meets: Every sampled item is marked clearly as revised, confirmed unaffected, or needing further checking — nothing left ambiguous.

rubric.criterion: It fits the time budget
rubric.meets: The whole review is scoped to fit inside roughly half a day, as this module argued for.

contentSections.body: This is the routine you can actually repeat every quarter — the version that fits inside a real, fixed time budget rather than the unbounded version that never gets started.
